en: He lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.
The Prāṇabhṛts are indeed the vital breaths; it is thus the vital breaths that he lays down. He lays them down in the first layer; for this first layer is the forepart of this Agni.
He places them in front; therefore these vital breaths are in front.
He lays them down ten by ten;
for there are ten vital breaths, and even when [something is done] many times, it is ten by ten—ten indeed.

He places them five times threefold, ten by ten; for he places these five animals, and in each animal there are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*); thus he bestows the vital breaths upon all of them. He places them so as not to be separated from the animals; he thereby bestows the vital breaths upon the animals without separating them from them. He places them on every side; [on] every side.
In this way, he bestows these vital breaths upon them.
Furthermore, as for why he lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital breaths departed from him, having become deities.
He said to them, "Come to me; restore to me that by which you have departed from me.
They replied, "Create that food for us, seeing which we may fast. "Then let us both create it," they said. "So be it.
Then those vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and Prajāpati created this food—these *prāṇabhṛt* bricks. 8.1.1 [4]
He places it in front with the words, "This one was in front. Agni, indeed, is in front;
as to why he says "in front" (puraḥ), they carry forth the fire towards the east and they attend upon it facing the east. And as to why he says "was" (bhuvaḥ), Agni, indeed, is "was" (bhūḥ).
"From fire indeed all this comes into being; for breath, having become fire, stood in front. He lays down that very form [of it]. Of it, the breath is the Bhauvāyana. 8.1.1.[5]

From that form of Agni he fashioned forth the vital breath (*prāṇa*); [with the words] "Spring is the source of the vital breath," he fashioned forth the spring season from the vital breath; [with the words] "The Gāyatrī belongs to spring," he fashioned forth the Gāyatrī metre from the spring season;
[with the words] "From the Gāyatrī, the Gāyatra," he fashioned forth the Gāyatra Sāman from the Gāyatrī metre.

From the Gāyatra he fashioned the Upāṃśu; thus from the Gāyatra sāman he fashioned the Upāṃśu cup. From the Upāṃśu [cup] he fashioned the Trivṛt; thus from the Upāṃśu cup he fashioned the Trivṛt stoma. From the Trivṛt he fashioned the Rathantara; thus from the Trivṛt stoma he fashioned the Rathantara pṛṣṭha. 8.1.1. [6]

"Vasiṣṭha the seer"—the breath indeed is Vasiṣṭha the seer; because he is the most excellent (*śreṣṭha*), he is Vasiṣṭha, and because he dwells most extensively (*vastṛtama*), he is likewise Vasiṣṭha. "With thee, taken by Prajāpati"—that is, created by Prajāpati.
With the words, "By thee," he takes up the vital breath; with "for the sake of offspring," he places the vital breath in front.

He lays them down separately, for whatever various desires exist in the vital breath, those he thereby bestows upon them. He settles them all at once, for he thus makes the vital breath one. Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely cut the vital breath asunder. This brick is threefold: the Yajus-formula and the settling.
The *sūdadohas* verse is threefold; Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—having made it so, he lays it down.
8.1.1 [7] Then on the south: "This one on the south is Viśvakarman. This wind here is indeed Viśvakarman.

For this [wind] blows and it makes all this; as to why he says "the right" (dakṣiṇā), therefore this wind blows most strongly toward the right. Mind, indeed, having become the wind, stood on the right; that very form he thus lays down. "Its mind belongs to Viśvakarman. 8.1.1. [8] Its mind belongs to Viśvakarman.

From that form, Mind fashioned Wind; from Mind, it fashioned the summer season, saying, "Summer is mental. From the summer season, it fashioned the Triṣṭubh meter, saying, "The Triṣṭubh belongs to summer.
From the Triṣṭubh meter, it fashioned the Svara-sāman, saying, "The Svara belongs to the Triṣṭubh meter."
He fashioned the Antaryāma cup from the Svāra [Sāman]. From the Svāra Sāman he fashioned the Antaryāma cup; from the Antaryāma cup he fashioned the Pañcadaśa Stoma;
from the Pañcadaśa Stoma he fashioned the Bṛhat Pṛṣṭha. 8.1.1. [9]

"Bharadvāja the seer"—the mind indeed is Bharadvāja the seer, and food is *vāja*. He who supports the mind supports food, which is *vāja*; therefore the mind is Bharadvāja the seer. [With the words] "By thee, taken by Prajāpati... [he takes it].

With the formula, "By thee, created by Prajāpati," he takes up the mind; with "for the sake of offspring," he causes the mind to descend to the south. He lays them down separately; whatever various desires are in the mind, those he thereby bestows upon it. He settles them all at once; thus he makes the mind one. Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely cleave the mind asunder. This brick is threefold (*trivṛt*); its [significance] has been explained.
The Kinsman (Bandhu) 8.1.2 [1]: Now, behind.
"This one behind is the all-encompassing" (ayam paścādviśvavyacāḥ). Yonder sun, indeed, is the all-encompassing, for when he—
Then all this speech arises; and as for why he says "behind," it is because the eye, having become the sun, stood behind; he thus lays down that very form. 8.1.2. [2]
"His eye was Vaiśvavyacas.
From that eye he fashioned out the form of Āditya;
"The rainy season is the offspring of the eye," so he fashioned the rainy season from the eye; "The Jagatī belongs to the rains," so he fashioned the Jagatī meter from the rainy season.
From the rainy season he fashioned the Ṛtu; from the Jagatī [meter] he fashioned the Ṛkṣama Sāman;
from the Ṛkṣama Sāman he fashioned the Śukra cup;
from the Śukra cup he fashioned the seventeenfold (saptadaśa) Stoma.
"From the seventeenfold [stoma], the Vairūpa," he said; from the seventeenfold stoma, he fashioned the Vairūpa Pṛṣṭha.
"Jamadagni the seer," he said; Jamadagni the seer is indeed the eye, for by means of it one sees the world and also reflects upon it.

Therefore, with the words, "Cakṣurjamadagni is the Ṛṣi; by thee, taken by Prajāpati," and "by thee, created by Prajāpati," he places the eye in the west with the words, "I take the eye for the sake of offspring. He lays them down separately; he thereby bestows those various desires that reside in the eye. He settles them once, making the eye one; and as to why he lays them down separately...
He would cause his eye to fail; he would cut it asunder. This is the threefold brick; its significance has been explained.
8.1.2. [4] Then on the north: "This one from the north is light. The quarters are indeed the north; as for why he says "from the north," it is because they are the most excellent (uttara).

Then, as for why he says "the quarters" (*diśaḥ*) after all this: the quarters are indeed the world of heaven (*svarga*). Having become the quarters, the ear stood to the north; that very form he now lays down.
Its [name] is "The Ear is of Heaven" (*tasya śrotraṃ sauvam*).
From that form he fashioned the ear, saying, "The autumnal [verse] is from the quarters";
from the ear he fashioned the season of autumn, saying, "The *anuṣṭubh* is autumnal";
from the season of autumn he fashioned the *anuṣṭubh* metre, saying, "The *aiḍa* [chant] is from the *anuṣṭubh*"; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre he fashioned the *aiḍa* *sāman*.
From the *aiḍa* [verse] he fashioned the *manthin* [cup]; from the *aiḍa* sāman he fashioned the *manthin* draught;
from the *manthin* [draught] he fashioned the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*ekaviṃśa-stoma*); from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form he fashioned the *vairāja* [sāman], the *pṛṣṭha* [laud]. 8.1.2. [6]
"Viśvāmitra is the seer.

Indeed, the ear is Viśvāmitra the seer; because by means of it one hears on all sides, and because everything becomes a friend (*mitra*) to it, therefore the ear is Viśvāmitra the seer. [With the words: "By thee, taken by Prajāpati..."
With the words, "By thee, created by Prajāpati," he places the ear on the south; with the words, "For the sake of offspring," he causes the ear to reach the north.
He lays them down separately; he thereby bestows those various desires that reside in the ear. He settles them once, for he makes the ear one.
Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely cut the ear asunder. This brick is threefold (*trivṛt*); its significance has been explained.
[The word] *bandhuḥ* [is used]. 8.1.2.[7] Now, regarding the middle:
"This one above is intelligence" (*iyam upari matiḥ*). Indeed, the moon is above; therefore, when he says "above" (*upari*), it is because it is indeed above.
Then, as to why he says, "The moon is thought" (*mati*): thought is indeed speech, for by means of speech one thinks all this;
and speech, having become the moon, stood above. He thus lays down that very form. Speech does not transcend it. 8.1.2. [8]

From that form, the moon, he fashioned speech; "Winter is [the essence] of speech," thus he fashioned the winter season from speech. "The *paṅkti* meter belongs to winter," thus he fashioned the *paṅkti* meter from the winter season. "The *nidhanavat* [Sāman] belongs to the *paṅkti*," thus the *nidhanavat* Sāman belongs to the *paṅkti* meter.
He fashioned the Āgrayaṇa cup from the Nidhanavat Sāman;

from the Āgrayaṇa cup he fashioned the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas; and from the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas he fashioned the Śākvara and Raivata Sāmans. From the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa [he fashioned them].
With the two *stomas*, the *śākvara* and *raivata*, he fashioned the two *pṛṣṭha* [chants].
"Viśvakarman is the seer (*ṛṣi*)," it is said;
for Viśvakarman the seer is indeed Speech (*vāc*), since by speech all this has been made.

Therefore, with the words, "O Viśvakarman, the seer, by thee taken by Prajāpati,"—that is to say, "by thee created by Prajāpati"—he takes up speech with the words, "I take up speech for the subjects," and thus he causes speech to flow forth from above. He lays down [the bricks] separately; whatever various desires are in speech, those he thereby bestows upon them. He settles them once; he thereby makes speech one. Now, as to why he lays them down separately...

If he were to let it settle, he would cut off his speech; this is that threefold brick, and its significance has been explained. This, indeed, is that food which the vital breaths and Prajāpati created; for the entire sacrifice is just this much, namely, the sacrifice.
"The food of the gods" (8.1.2.[11]).
He lays them down ten by ten;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is indeed all food.

He places all this food entirely within him; he places them on every side, for he thus bestows all this food upon him from every direction. These indeed are the Virāj bricks; they sustain these vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Because they sustain the vital breaths, they are called *prāṇabhṛt* (breath-sustainers). 8.1.3. [1]

Regarding this they ask: "What are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)? What are the sustainers of the vital breaths (*prāṇabhṛt*)? The vital breaths themselves are the vital breaths; the limbs are the sustainers of the vital breaths, for the limbs indeed sustain the vital breaths.

But the vital breaths are the vital breaths, and food is the sustainer of the vital breaths, for food indeed sustains the vital breaths. Regarding this they ask: "How do all these [verses] of his become related to Prajāpati? [The answer is: "Because he recites them over all [the bricks]."
"By thee, taken by Prajāpati"—thus indeed do all these [verses] of his become related to Prajāpati.

Regarding this they say: "Since they chant the *stotra* for a cup that has already been drawn, and then recite the *śastra*, why does he place the *ṛc*s and *sāman*s before the cups? [The answer is: "The completion is indeed the end of the ritual action."
It should be observed that by means of the *ṛc*, the cup is indeed drawn; upon the *ṛc* the *sāman* is sung.

Therefore, this which he places before the cups—the *ṛcs* and the *sāmans*—is that very thing for him. And as for what occurs after the cups—the *stotra* and the *śastra*—that too is his subsequent portion following the cups.
He lays down the *stomas* and the *pṛṣṭhas*.

Regarding this, they say: "Since these three—the cup (*graha*), the chant (*stotra*), and the recitation (*śastra*)—are performed together, and here he lays down only the cup and the chant, how is it that the recitation is also laid down for him here? Whatever is the chant, that indeed is the recitation; in those [verses]...

He indeed praises [the *stotra*], and he likewise recites the *anustotra* after it; thus, even here, his *śastra* becomes properly established. Regarding this, they say: "Just as one speaks of a son in relation to a father, so does he speak of the first three [verses]; but why then does he transition from the *ṛc* to the *sāman*? The *sāman* is indeed the husband of the *ṛc*; therefore, if he were to speak there also as of a son in relation to a father, it would be as follows...
He should say to his son, "Be such as I am," and likewise to his grandson; for from that [lineage] it passes on to those two. Why does he extend it thrice?
He extends it to the father, the son, and the grandson; therefore, he gives to them only one [offering].
Now, as for those which he places in front...

Now, those [reeds] which are in the east are the sustainers of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); they are the sustainers of sight and the sustainers of the out-breath (*apāna*). Those which are on the south are the sustainers of the mind (*manas*); they are the sustainers of the diffused breath (*vyāna*). Those which are on the north are the sustainers of hearing (*śrotra*); they are the sustainers of the up-breath (*udāna*). And those which are in the middle are the sustainers of speech (*vāc*); they are the sustainers of the equalizing breath (*samāna*). 8.1.3. [7]
Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus indeed lay down other bricks called Apānabhṛts, Vyānabhṛts, Udānabhṛts, Samānabhṛts,
Cakṣurbhṛts, Manobhṛts, Śrotrabhṛts, and Vāgbhṛts; but one should not do so.
One should perform this very day, for it is here that all these forms are laid down.
Having first laid them down in the east, he then lays them down in the west;
for the out-breath (prāṇa), having become the in-breath (apāna), [proceeds] from the tips of the fingers.

The out-breath (*apāna*) indeed moves about, having become the in-breath (*prāṇa*), from the tips of the fingers; thus it moves about. Now, when he lays down [bricks] behind after having first laid them down in front, he thereby extends and joins these two breaths together. Therefore, these two breaths are continuous and joined.
Then, having laid them down on the south, he lays them down on the north.
For the *vyāna*, having become the *udāna*, circulates as far as the tips of the fingers;
and the *udāna*, having become the *vyāna*, circulates as far as the tips of the fingers. This is why [he places them] on the south.
Having placed [the first], he places these two on the north; he thus extends and joins these two vital breaths together. Therefore, these two vital breaths are continuous and joined.
Then, those which he places in the middle—

He places that vital air (prāṇa) within the range of the two *retaḥsic* bricks. The two *retaḥsic* are indeed the ribs, and the ribs are in the middle; thus he places this vital air in him right in the middle. He places it on all sides;
thus he places this vital air in him on every side. Moreover, this is the vital air of the anus.

He places them all around the navel, both lengthwise and crosswise; therefore these vital breaths in the body run both lengthwise and crosswise. He places them so that they touch one another; he thereby extends the vital breaths and joins them together.
Therefore these vital breaths are continuous and interconnected. 8.1.4. [1]
Some place them after having offered a man [as a victim], saying:
"This indeed is the vital breath (prāṇa); these bricks support it;
since they support the vital breath, they are called 'vital-breath-supporters' (prāṇabhṛt). One should not do so; for this golden one here is indeed the vital breath itself.

This person is his very self, as far as this fire has been laid out here. For if these [fuel-sticks] were not to reach its limbs, then the vital breath would not reach that limb of his; and whatever limb the vital breath does not reach, that indeed either withers or decays. Therefore, he [lays down] these.
One should place them by handing them over within the enclosing stones; then, those which one places in the middle—with these his body is filled, and they are indeed not separated from this [body].
Regarding this, they say: "This one is *Purobhuvas*, this one is *Viśvakarman* on the south, and this one is *Viśvavyacas* on the west."

"This one from the north, the thought above"—thus the quarters are now recited over. Now, why does he lay them down in diagonal positions? The Prāṇabhṛt bricks are indeed the vital breaths; if he were to lay them down facing the quarters directly, this vital breath would indeed circulate only forward and backward. But since they are thus recited over...
He places them transversely on the directions; therefore this breath, though moving forward, traverses all the limbs and the entire self transversely.
This Agni is indeed that animal.
Thus, all this entire conditioned world is his;
those which he places in front are his two arms, those which he places behind are his two thighs, and those which he places in the middle are the trunk.
He places them in the region of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; for the two *retaḥsic*s are the ribs, and the ribs are in the middle.
For this Self places [the bricks] on all sides from the middle; for this Self is indeed on all sides.

8.1.4.[4] Regarding this they say: "Since in the preceding groups he places one *stoma* and one *pṛṣṭha* each, why does he here place two *stomas* and two *pṛṣṭhas*? [The answer is: This is his very self; he thus places the self within the self.

He makes it the eldest, the most excellent, and the most powerful of the limbs; therefore, this self (ātman) is the eldest, the most excellent, and the most powerful of the limbs. 8.1.4 [5]. Regarding this they say: "How does this fire of his become entirely and completely consecrated in every single brick?"

The marrow is the *yajus*, the bone is the brick, the flesh is the settling-place (*sādana*), the skin is the *kṣūdadohas*, the hair is the *yajus* for the loose soil, and the food is the loose soil itself. In this way, indeed, this Agni of his becomes entirely and completely prepared in every single brick. This is that Agni who possesses a full lifespan.
He who knows this Agni as the one that encompasses all life-span indeed reaches the full span of life. Now, therefore, concerning the contracting and expanding [of the altar]:
some [teachers] say it is already built when it has been piled together.
They touch it with the words, "By contracting and extending," for this Agni is indeed an animal; when an animal contracts its limbs and extends them, then it performs its strength by means of them.
"Thou art the *saṃvatsara* (the full year), thou art the *parivatsara* (the recurring year)."
You are the Idāvatsara; you are the Iḍvatsara; you are the Vatsara.
May your dawns prosper; may your days and nights prosper; may your half-months prosper; may your months prosper;
may your seasons prosper; may your year prosper. For departure and for arrival, move together and move forward. You are indeed the well-winged one.
"By that deity, may you sit firm like Aṅgiras"—thus [he says]. Śāṭyāyani also used to say:
"One indeed heard the cracking of the two wings of this [altar] when it was touched with this [formula]."
"Therefore, one should touch him with this very [formula]," so it is said.
Now, Svarhin Nagnajit—or rather, Nagnajit Gāndhāra—used to say: "The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed..."
Bending and extending—that limb in which the vital breath (*prāṇa*) resides, he bends together and extends forth.

He should anoint it from the outside while it is already bent together; thus he places the vital breath—the bending and extending—into it, so that it bends together and extends forth. That very bending and extending is what he spoke of when he said, "that indeed."

But he who is a kinsman of royalty spoke thus: "Even if a hundred or even a thousand men were to strike from the outside, they would certainly not take away his breath; for that which is the breath in one's own self is indeed the breath itself. Thus, when he lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks, he bestows upon him the breath that consists of contraction and expansion."

In this manner he bends it together and stretches it out; then he lays down two *lokampṛṇā* bricks in that corner; the significance of these is explained above. He scatters loose soil (*purīṣa*); the significance of that is explained above. 8.2.1 [1] He lays down the second layer.

They said, "Discern ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek upwards from here! They said, "Discern ye!"—by which they meant, "
While reflecting, they perceived this second layer: that which is above the earth and below the atmosphere.
This world seemed to them, in their minds, as if unstable and as if without support.
They said to the Aśvins: [8.2.1.3]

"You two are indeed the two Brahmans and the two physicians; lay down this second layer for us. "What will become of us from that? [The gods replied,] "You two alone shall be the Adhvaryus for our Agnicayana here. "So be it," they said, and the Aśvins laid down this second layer for them.

Therefore they say, "The Aśvins alone are the Adhvaryus among the gods. He lays it down with the words: "Firmly seated, of firm birth, thou art firm. For that which is stable and that which is established—

Then, either this world was indeed unstable for them, or it appeared as if unstable and without support in their minds; having made that very [world] firm and stable, they established it with the words, "Sit thou on the firm, stable womb well.
"Sit thou on the firm womb well"—this means "sit thou firmly on the womb well. "Accepting the first banner of the Ukhyā fire"—this refers to this [fire].
Or [it is] the fire in the *ukhā* pot; this first layer is its first sign (*ketu*).
"May they enjoy it"—this refers to that. "O Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, may you settle it here"—for the Aśvins were indeed the two Adhvaryus who deposited it.
"The nest-like, the butter-filled, the wise one. 8.2.1.[5]
"The second layer is indeed like a nest; 'Sit on the pleasant seat of the earth!'—the first layer is indeed the earth; thus he means, 'Sit on her auspicious, pleasant seat.
'May the Rudras and the Vasus sing thy praises!'—this means, 'may these deities sing thy praises. 'Swell these prayers!'"
"For prosperity," he says; this means "O Brahman, sit here for prosperity. "O Aśvins, as Adhvaryus, establish yourselves here"—for the two Aśvins indeed established themselves as the two Adhvaryus.
"With your own powers, O Father of Power, may you sit here."

"Sit here by your own power"—this means "sit here with your own vigor. "For the great joy of the gods' assembly"—this means "for the great favor and the great joy of the gods. "Be like a father to the son, very gracious"—just as a father is pleasant and very gracious to his son, so be very gracious. "Enter with a body that is easy of access"—the body (*tanū*) is indeed the self (*ātman*).
"Enter with your own self through your own entrance"—this [he says]; "May the two Aśvins, the Adhvaryus, settle you here"—for the two Aśvins indeed were the Adhvaryus who deposited [the bricks];
"Thou art the soil of the earth."

"The earth, indeed, is the first layer; its *purīṣa* (filling) is this second [layer], which is called 'water'—that is to say, 'sap. 'May all the gods chant for thee,' that is to say, 'may all the gods chant for thee. 'Seated here upon the back of the *stomas*, rich in ghee,' refers to those *stomas* which he will spread out upon her."

With these [verses], this [offering] has the *stoma* as its back; "win for us wealth accompanied by progeny" means "win for us wealth that is accompanied by progeny"; "may the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, settle you here"—for it was the Aśvins who established the two Adhvaryus. 8.2.1. [8]
These are the quarters.
He places them within the range of the two Retahsic bricks; for these two, the Retahsic, are indeed these two worlds, and thus he places the quarters within these two worlds.
Therefore, the quarters are within these two. He places them on all sides; thus he places the quarters on all sides, and therefore the quarters are on all sides.
He places them facing toward all directions; therefore the quarters face toward all.
He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for the quarters are indeed separate.
Then he lays down the fifth brick belonging to the quarters.
That which is the upward direction is indeed consecration (dīkṣā); that upward direction is yonder sun.
It is yonder sun that he thus lays down. He lays it down within the southern direction;
he thereby places yonder sun between himself and the southern direction. Therefore, he moves between himself and the southern direction. 8.2.1 [10]
"On the back of Aditi I set thee down"—Aditi is indeed this earth; he thus establishes him upon this very foundation. "The supporter of the atmosphere, the prop of the quarters, the sovereign lady."

"Of the worlds"—for he is indeed the supporter of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), the prop of the quarters, and the lord of the worlds. "Thou art the wave, the drop of the waters"—the wave is indeed essence. "Viśvakarman is thy seer"—Viśvakarman is Prajāpati;
thus it means, "Thou art created by Prajāpati. "May the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, settle thee here."
"Thou"—for the Aśvins, as Adhvaryus, placed [the two bricks] there. Furthermore, as to why he lays down these Aśvinī bricks:
when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took him and departed; of him—
That which was above the foundation and below the middle, the Aśvins took that from him and stood apart.
He said to them:
"Come to me; restore to me that by which you two have raised me."
"Let us go," they said. "What will come of that for us? [The other replied,] "This [sacrifice] shall belong to me, with you two as its deities. "So be it," they said;
and so the Aśvins established this [offering] for him. 8.2.1 [13]

Now, these which are the five *Aśvinī* bricks—this is that very self of his; and in that he lays them down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this self of his. Therefore, he lays these down here. 8.2.1.[14]
"Of firm foundation, of firm origin, thou art firm.
For that which is stable and firmly established is "firm" (*dhruva*);
yet this [body] of his was, as it were, unstable and unfirm for himself; therefore, having now made it stable and firm, he says this.
They two responded with [the verses]:
"The nest-maker, rich in ghee, the wise one.
For this [fire-altar] of his is indeed like a nest for the self.

"By your own skill, O skillful one, sit down here"—it is for the sake of non-destruction that he says this; "you are the soil (purīṣa) of this self on earth," for this [brick] of his self is indeed connected with the soil. With the *retaḥsic* bricks at its boundary: the *retaḥsic* bricks are the ribs, and thus this [brick] of his self is joined with the ribs. He lays it down on all sides, for it is on all sides.

For the Aśvins restored this to him from themselves. 8.2.1.[16] Now he lays down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons that he lays down—namely, Śukra and Śuci.

"Summer and the rainy season" are the names of these two; it is by means of these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once; thus he makes the season one. As to why he lays these two down here—

This Agni is the year; he is these worlds, for the year is these worlds. That which is above the earth and below the atmosphere is his second layer; that is his summer season. It is because of this that he lays down these two bricks here. 8.2.1 [18]
Moreover, as to why he lays these down here:
this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year. That part of him which is above the foundation and below the middle is his second layer; that is his summer.
The seasons are these; in that he lays these down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this body of his;
therefore he lays these down here. 8.2.2. [1] Now he lays down the Vaiśvadevī bricks.
This indeed is that second layer which the Aśvins then deposited for these [worlds];
having deposited it, they came to possess all this, whatever exists here.
Those gods said:

"The Aśvins indeed have become this entire world; find out how we too may be here. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek it so that we too may be here. While meditating, they saw these bricks dedicated to the Viśvedevas. 8.2.2. [3]
They said, "The Aśvins indeed became this entire world; let us pile up the layers of the Aśvins in accordance with the Aśvins.
They piled up the layers of the Aśvins in accordance with the Aśvins. Therefore, they call this layer the Āśvinī layer.
Therefore, just as was the result of the previous layers, so it is with these; for by means of the Aśvins they laid down the layer following the thought of the Aśvins.
And as to why he lays down the Vaiśvadevī bricks:
those Viśve Devas who saw this second layer, they [are they].
With this same essence they obtained them; it is these very ones that he now lays down. These are all creatures.

He lays them down in the vicinity of the two *retahsic* bricks; for the two *retahsic* are these two worlds, and thus he places the creatures within these two worlds. Therefore, creatures exist within these two worlds.
He lays them down on every side; he thereby places creatures on every side; therefore, creatures exist on every side in the quarters.
He places them around; he thereby establishes progeny in the quarters, and therefore progeny exist in all the quarters.
Furthermore, as for why he places the Vaiśvadevī bricks: from Prajāpati, when he had become relaxed, all creatures emerged from his middle.
They emerged from this womb and entered him when that [part] of his own self had been restored.
That Prajāpati who fell apart is indeed this very Agni who is being built; and those creatures that issued from him—

They emerged from the middle; these are indeed the Vaiśvadeva bricks. When he lays these down, he causes those very offspring that emerged from his middle to enter into him. He places them on the level of the two *retahsic* bricks; for the two *retahsic* are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle. Thus, he causes these offspring to enter into him from the middle, on every side.
He places them down; verily, he causes all these creatures to enter into him from every side. And as to why he places the Vaiśvadevī bricks:
when that part of his own self had been restored, Prajāpati [performed this].
"He desired, 'May I create offspring; may I procreate. Having become yoked together with the seasons, the waters, the vital breaths, the year, and the two Aśvins, he procreated these offspring.
In the same way, this sacrificer, having become yoked together with these deities, procreates these offspring. Therefore, in all [the formulas], the word 'sajūs' (in unison) recurs. 8.2.2. [8]
"In harmony with the seasons"—thereby he generated the seasons;
indeed, having become united with the seasons, he generated them. "In harmony with the ordinances"—the ordinances are the waters, for by the waters all this is ordained; indeed, by the waters...

"Having become united, he procreated with the gods," thus he procreated the gods; for that which they call "the gods" (devāḥ), [he said] "united with the gods who are the sustainers of life" (*vayonādhāḥ*). The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the gods who are the sustainers of life, for by the vital breaths all this is bound together as a web of knowledge (*vayuna*).
Moreover, the meters (*chandāṃsi*) are indeed the gods who are the sustainers of life, for by the meters all this is bound together as a web of knowledge.

Having indeed become yoked with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he generated [the fire] with the words, "For Agni Vaiśvānara, thee! Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; having indeed become yoked with the year, he generated [it]. With the words, "O Aśvins, Adhvaryus, settle him here," he generated [it] having indeed become yoked with the two Aśvins. 8.2.2. [9]
With "In harmony with the Vasus," [he offers] on the south; thereby he generated the Vasus. With "In harmony with the Rudras," on the west;
thereby he generated the Rudras. With "In harmony with the Ādityas," on the north; thereby he generated the Ādityas. With "In harmony with all the gods... [he offers].

Thus, from above, he brought forth the Viśve Devas. They have the same opening and the same conclusion, but differ in the middle. As for their having the same opening and the same conclusion: it was by means of identical deities at the beginning and at the end that he, having become united with them, brought them forth; and as for their differing in the middle: it is because offspring in the middle are diverse.
He generated [the breaths]. 8.2.3.[1] Now he lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.
Regarding this, the gods said, "Reflect ye!"—that is to say, "Seek a layer! indeed.
Being conscious of that, they saw Vāyu himself as the layer; they placed him therein, and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places him therein.
He lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.

Vital breath is indeed wind; he thus places wind in this [brick]. It is on the level of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; these two are indeed the *retaḥsic*; he thus places wind in these two. Therefore, wind is in these two. He lays them down on all sides;
he thus places wind on all sides. Therefore, wind is on all sides. On all sides, facing together.
He places the wind correctly on all sides; therefore, having become correct on all sides, it blows from all directions.
He places the *diśyā* bricks; he thus places the wind in the quarters, and therefore the wind is in all the quarters.
Furthermore, as to why he places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks.
Verily, he bestows vital breaths upon these very offspring;

he places them immediately after those belonging to the Viśvedevas, and thus he bestows vital breaths upon the offspring without interruption: "Protect my out-breath; protect my in-breath; protect my diffused breath; illumine my eye with wide vision; [protect] my hearing."
"Recite the verses," he says; thus he bestows these very vital breaths (*prāṇa*) that have been so fashioned.
8.2.3.[4] Then he lays down the *apasyā* bricks. For the gods said, "Meditate!"—that is to say, "Seek a layer (*citi*)."
Being conscious of that, they saw the rain itself as a layer; they placed it in him, and in the same way, he now places it in him.
He lays down the *apasyā* bricks.
Water, indeed, is rain; verily, he thus bestows rain upon this [sacrificer]. On the level of the two Retahsic bricks; these two are the Retahsic;
he thus bestows rain upon these two worlds. Therefore it rains upon these two. He places them on every side;
he thus bestows rain on every side. Therefore it rains on every side. He places them facing each other on every side; he thus makes it face him from every side.

He bestows rain; therefore, having become perfectly level on all sides, it rains from all directions. He places them along the Vāyavyā bricks; he thus bestows rain upon the wind. Therefore, whichever direction the wind goes, the rain follows that direction. 8.2.3 [6]
And again, as to why he lays down the Apasyās:

it is in these very vital breaths that he thereby places water. He lays them down separated from the Prāṇabhṛts; thus he places water not separated from the vital breaths. Moreover, water is indeed food; [thus he places] food not separated [from the breaths].

"Thou dost bestow food upon their vital breaths; swell the waters, quicken the plants; protect the two-footed and the four-footed; send down rain from heaven"—it is these very well-ordered waters that he thereby places within them.
Then he lays down the *candasyā* bricks.

The gods indeed said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi). While reflecting, they saw the animals as the layer; they placed them in this [altar], and in the same way, he now places them in this one. 8.2.3. [8]
He lays down the *candas* (metres). The *candas* are indeed cattle; verily, he thus bestows cattle upon him. He lays them down on all sides; he thus bestows cattle on every side.
Therefore, cattle are on every side. He lays them down following the *apasyās*; [he places them] in the waters.
He thereby establishes the cattle; therefore, when it rains, then the cattle find firm support.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Chandasyā bricks:
from Prajāpati, when he was relaxed, the cattle departed, having become the metres (chandas).
Having become the Gāyatrī metre, he obtained them through vital power; for that which the Gāyatrī obtained was the swiftest among the metres.
Having become that, Prajāpati obtained these animals through vital power: "Vital power is the head. 8.2.3. [10]
"Prajāpati is indeed the head; he became the *vaya* (age/strength).
'Prajāpati is the metre'—thus Prajāpati himself became the metre.
'The *kṣatra* (sovereignty) is the *vaya*. 8.2.3.[11]

Prajāpati is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*); he became the *vaya* called "Mayanda-chandas. That which is undefined (*anirukta*) is the Mayanda; Prajāpati is indeed undefined, and thus Prajāpati himself became the *chandas*.
"The Support is the *vaya*. 8.2.3 [12]
Prajāpati is indeed the support; he became the bird.
"The overlord is the metre"—Prajāpati is indeed the overlord, and Prajāpati himself became the metre.
"Viśvakarman is the bird. 8.2.3 [13]
Prajāpati is indeed Viśvakarman; he became Vaya and the Parameṣṭhin, the metre.
Water is Prajāpati the Parameṣṭhin, for they abide in the highest place. Prajāpati himself became the Parameṣṭhin, the metre. 8.2.3 [14]
These, indeed, are the four stages of life and the four meters; that makes eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
This is that Gāyatrī which, having become that, Prajāpati reached these animals by means of their age. Therefore, one reaches an aged animal by means of its age.

Thus they say; therefore, in all [the verses], the word "bird" (vayas) recurs. Now, those cattle which went out from him—these are the fifteen [verses] above. Cattle are indeed a thunderbolt (vajra), and the thunderbolt is fifteenfold. Therefore, he who possesses cattle truly strikes away evil; the thunderbolt indeed strikes away his evil.
Therefore, in whichever direction one leads a sacrificial animal, it follows that very direction ordained by the *vajra*.
8.2.4.[1] "May the goat [attain] vigor"—with this he bestowed vigor upon the goat. "The *candas* with two feet"—the *candas* with two feet are indeed the *ekapadā* (one-footed) verses;
having become *ekapadās*, the goats went forth. 8.2.4.[2]
‘Vṛṣṇir vayaḥ’—by this he obtained *vṛṣṇi* as his vigor. ‘Viśālaṃ chandaḥ’—the *viśāla* meter is indeed the two-footed; having become two-footed, the birds flew up. 8.2.4 [3]
"Puruṣa, vaya!"—he attained the Puruṣa by means of *vaya*. "Tandra, chandas"—*tandra* is indeed the *chandas* Paṅkti;
having become the Paṅkti, the Puruṣas departed. 8.2.4. [4]
"The tiger by its age"—he attained the tiger by its age. "The invincible meter"—the invincible meter is indeed the *virāj*;
the *virāj* is food, and food is invincible. Having become the *virāj*, the tigers went forth. 8.2.4 [5]
"The lion is the age"—thus they attained the lion through their age. "The *cadi* is the metre"—the *cadi* metre is indeed the *aticandā*; for the *aticandā* encompasses all metres.
Having become *aticandās*, the lions stepped forth; from that point on, they were indeed specifically named.
He lays down the defined metres as animals:
"The two-year-old ox as age; the Bṛhatī metre as age"—for having become the Bṛhatī, it attained the age of a two-year-old ox.
The draft-oxen stepped forth. "The bull, the age"—with this [formula], they reached the bull by means of the age. "The *kakubh* metre"—having become the *kakubh*, the bull [was reached].
They ascended with the words, "The bull by age.
He attained the bull by age; [with the words] "The *satobṛhatī* metre," it indeed became the *satobṛhatī*.
The bulls stepped forth.
"Anaḍvān vayaḥ" (the ox is the age);
he attained the age through the ox. "Paṅktiś chandaḥ" (the Paṅkti is the metre); having indeed become the Paṅkti, [he attained it] through the ox.
They stepped forth with the words, "The cow, the bird.
By means of its age, it attained the cow; by means of the *jagatī* metre, it became the *jagatī*, and thus [attained] the cows.
They stepped forward.
"The three-year-old as age"—he attains the three-year-old by means of its age; "the *triṣṭubh* as meter"—having become the *triṣṭubh*, he [attains] the three-year-old.
They stepped forth:
"The two-year-old steed," [he said];
he attained the two-year-old steed through its age. "The Virāj metre," [he said]; having become the Virāj, [he attained] the two-year-old steed.
They stepped out [saying], "The fivefold age.
He attained the fivefold age with his age; [thinking] "the Gāyatrī metre," he became the Gāyatrī and [attained] the fivefold age.
They stepped forth with the words, "The three-year-old calf as age.
He attained the three-year-old calf by means of age; "the *uṣṇih* as meter"—having indeed become the *uṣṇih*, he [attained] the three-year-old calf.
They stepped forth.
"The four-year-old steed"—having attained the age of a four-year-old steed, he became the *anuṣṭubh* meter; having become the *anuṣṭubh*, he [proceeded].
The four-year-old oxen went up first. 8.2.4.[16] These indeed are those animals;
those which Prajāpati obtained by means of the bird. He indeed took the animal first, and then the bird.
And the Moon, having encompassed them with his age and with the *candas*, took them into himself and made them his own;
in the very same way, this [sacrificer], having encompassed these [bricks] with their age and with the *candas*, takes them into himself and makes them his own.
This Agni is indeed that animal.

Thus, all this entire conditioned [universe] belongs to him: those bricks which he lays down in front are his head; those on the south and north are his body; and those behind are his tail. 8.2.4 [18]
He indeed places [the bricks] first in the east;

for the head of one being born is born first. Then, having placed them on the south, he places them on the north, thinking, "May this body be born together with [the head]. Then [he places] the tail in the west.
In the end, for one who is being born, [the body] is born. 8.2.4.[19] Therefore, those which are the longest meters and those which are the largest animals, he places in the middle.

He places that most excellent animal facing the middle; therefore, the animal is most excellent facing the middle. Then, those animals which are most vigorous, he places on the south side; he thereby makes the right half of the animal more vigorous, and therefore the right half of the animal is more vigorous. 8.2.4 [20]
He makes the two front halves and the two rear halves the smallest;
because those four were [the largest], they are the smallest; and because he places the smallest animals here, therefore these are the smallest. And the front half...

And he makes the two buttocks of the animal from that hind-quarter; therefore both the fore-part and the hind-part of the animal are the two buttocks, and therefore the animal stands up by means of the fore-part and sits down by means of the hind-part. Then he lays down two *lokampṛṇā* bricks in this corner; the significance of those two is above, and then there is the loose earth (*purīṣa*).
He scatters [the earth]; the significance of this has been explained above.
He lays down the third layer.
Indeed, having built the second layer, the gods ascended to that which is above it.
That which is on this side of the earth and on the other side of the atmosphere—that very thing they prepared and ascended.
They said, "Reflect (cetayadhvam)!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citim icata)"; that is, "Seek upwards from here.
While reflecting, they saw the atmosphere itself as the third layer, the Bṛhatī. That world appeared pleasing to them.
They said to Indra and Agni, "Do you two lay down this third layer for us. They asked, "What will become of us from that?
[Indra and Agni replied,] "You two shall be the most excellent among us. Saying, "So be it," Indra and Agni [bestowed] this [layer] upon them.
They laid down the third layer; therefore they say that Indra and Agni alone are the most excellent among the gods. He lays them down with [the formulas dedicated to] Indra and Agni;
he settles them with Viśvakarman, for Indra and Agni are indeed Viśvakarman.
They did not perceive this third layer; therefore, he lays it down with [bricks] for Indra and Agni and settles them with Viśvakarman.
Furthermore, as to why he lays them down with [bricks] for Indra and Agni and settles them with Viśvakarman: the deities abandoned Prajāpati when he was shattered.
Having taken it, he stepped away; then Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman took the middle part and stepped away.
He said to them:
"Come to me and give back to me that by which you have departed from me. They replied: "What would we have from that?"

"It shall be so; this [brick] of mine shall belong to you as its deity. "So be it," they said. Then Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman placed that very [brick] within him. Now, that which is this middle *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated) brick—
This is that very self of his; when he places this brick here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this self of his.
Therefore, he places this brick here:
"O Indra and Agni, [place you] unshakable..."
"Strengthen the brick, you two"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance.
"With your back you push apart heaven and earth and the intermediate space"—for with her back she indeed pushes apart heaven, earth, and the intermediate space. 8.3.1 [9]
"May Viśvakarman settle thee"—
for Viśvakarman indeed perceived this third layer; "on the back of the atmosphere, wide-extending, spreading"— for this is indeed the back of the atmosphere.
"Make the atmosphere spacious and wide; steady the atmosphere, do not harm the atmosphere"—this means "steady yourself, do not harm yourself.
For the sake of all out-breathing and in-breathing. 8.3.1 [10]

"For Vyāna, for Udāna"—the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇā*) is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the vital breath serves as a support for all this; "for stability, for movement"—these worlds are indeed the naturally perforated bricks, and these worlds are stability and movement. "May Vāyu protect you"—that is, "may Vāyu guard you"; "with great well-being."

With the verse, "With great well-being," he means "with that most peaceful heart-covering"; having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula—the significance of which has already been explained—and then he sings the *sāman*; its significance will follow later.
Then he lays down the regional bricks (*diśyā*).

The regional bricks (diśyā) are indeed the quarters; it is the quarters that he thus lays down. Those very quarters by which Vāyu approached from there, being unseparated [from him], those he now lays down.
And those same ones he lays down in front, together with a bunch of darbha grass and the clod-bricks; for yonder sun is these [bricks], and he thus [places] yonder sun.
He piles them up in the quarters; he piles them in the quarters. If they were to remain right there, they would be outside;

for this work of the fire-altar which is done prior to the lotus-leaf is indeed outside the womb. When he brings them here and lays them down, he establishes them in their womb, upon the lotus-leaf. Thus they do not become external, and they are placed without any interval.

He lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks. The middle *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*); by placing them so as not to be separated from it, he establishes the quarters from the intermediate region. He places them one above the other; thus he establishes the quarters from the intermediate region. He places them on the level of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; these two are indeed the *retaḥsic*; thus he establishes the quarters upon these two. Therefore, the quarters are established upon these two.
He lays them down on every side; thus he establishes the quarters on every side. Therefore the quarters are on every side.
He lays them down facing each other on every side; therefore the quarters face each other on every side.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *diśyā* bricks.

The meters are indeed the quarters: the Gāyatrī is the eastern quarter, the Triṣṭubh the southern, the Jagatī the western, the Anuṣṭubh the northern, and the Paṅkti the upward direction. The meters are indeed cattle; the middle layer is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Thus he places cattle in the intermediate space. Therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode. 8.3.1 [13]
Moreover, as to why he lays down the *diśyā* bricks:

the quarters are indeed the *candāṃsi* (metres), and the metres are cattle; cattle are food, and the middle layer is the middle. Thus, he places that food in the middle. These [bricks] are not separated from the *svayamātṛṇā*.

He lays them down. The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed the vital breath; he thus places food not separated from the vital breath. He places them on the north; he thus places food higher than the vital breath. At the level of the two *retaḥsic* bricks: the two *retaḥsic* are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle;
verily, he thus places food in his very center. He places them on all sides; verily, he thus places food in him from every side.
He establishes [them]. 8.3.1.[14] "Thou art the sovereign, the eastern quarter;
thou art the far-shining, the southern quarter; thou art the self-ruling, the western quarter; thou art the unassailable, the northern quarter."
"You are the great mistress of the quarters; 'the quarter'—these are their names. By mentioning their names, he thus lays them down.
He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for the quarters are separate.
Then he lays down the *viśvajyotis* (all-light) brick.

Vāyu indeed is the Viśvajyotis of the middle; for Vāyu is indeed the universal light in the world of the atmosphere. It is Vāyu whom he thus lays down. He lays it down immediately adjacent to the bricks belonging to the quarters; he thereby places Vāyu in the quarters; therefore [he is present] in all the quarters.
The Wind (vāyu).
Now, as to why he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick:
offspring, indeed, are the Viśvajyotis; for offspring are truly the universal light.

He thus lays down procreation itself. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the two regional bricks; he thereby places offspring in the quarters; therefore, there are offspring in all the quarters.
"May Viśvakarman settle you," [he says].
For Viśvakarman perceived this third layer,
"the luminous one upon the back of the atmosphere," for indeed, Vāyu, the luminous one, is upon the back of the atmosphere;
it is for the sake of every out-breath and in-breath.
"For Vyāna"—the Viśvajyotis is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), for the vital breath provides light to all this;
"grant universal light"—that is, "grant all light"; "Vāyu is your overlord"—he makes Vāyu its overlord.
Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has already been explained.
8.3.2.[5] Now he lays down the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons that he lays down—namely, Nabhas and [Nabhasya].

Nabhasya and [Nabhas] are the names of the two rainy seasons; it is by these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once, thereby making the season one. He lays them down upon *avakā* plants and covers them with *avakā* plants; for *avakā* plants are water, and thus he places water in this season.

He places them; therefore, it rains most abundantly during this season. 8.3.2.[6] Then the two northern ones: "Food and strength, the autumnal seasons"—these are the names of these two. By means of these very names he thus lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months; he settles them once, thereby [unifying] that single season.
He makes openings and lays down *avakā* plants. The *avakā* plants are indeed water; he thus places water at the front of this season.
Therefore, it rains at the front of this season, but not from above. He does not cover it over from above; therefore, it does not rain in that same way from above. 8.3.2. [7]
Now, as to why he lays these down here: this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds.

Of that [year], the middle layer is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa); the rainy season and the autumn are its intermediate space. Therefore, when he lays these down here, he restores to him that which belongs to his own self; that is why he lays these down.
Here he lays them down. And as to why he lays these down here: this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year; of him—

The middle layer itself is the middle consciousness; the rainy season and autumn are the two intermediate seasons. In that he lays these [bricks] here, he thereby restores to this body whatever of it belongs to those [seasons]. Therefore, he lays them here. These four seasonal bricks he lays in the middle layer; he lays two in each of the other layers.
Cattle indeed have four feet; the middle layer is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); he thus places cattle in the intermediate space.
Therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode. Furthermore, as to why there are four: cattle indeed have four feet; cattle are food; the middle [layer] is the middle.
He places that food in the middle with the word *citiḥ*.
Furthermore, as to why there are four:
the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) consists of four syllables, and [the other] consists of two syllables.
The other layers are as extensive as the intermediate space; having made them so, he lays them down.
And as to why there are four:
this Agni is an animal; he thus makes the animal widest at its middle.

Therefore, the animal is most excellent for the middle layer. 8.3.2.[13] Now, these are the four seasonal bricks; the *viśvajyotis* is the fifth. There are five regional bricks; that makes ten. The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food. The middle layer is the middle; thus, he places that food in the middle. These...
He places the *svayamātṛṇā* bricks without any interval; for the *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed breath.
Thus he places food without interval from breath. He places them one above the other; thus he places food higher and higher than breath. Then he places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks.

The vital breaths are indeed the Prāṇabhṛts; it is the vital breaths that he thus lays down. They are ten in number, for there are ten vital breaths. He lays them down in the front part, for these vital breaths are in the front. With the words, "Protect my life-span!
Bestow light upon me!"—light is indeed the vital breath—he thereby says, "Bestow the vital breath upon me. These are laid down immediately after the Ṛtavyās.
He lays them down. Vāyu is indeed breath; thus he establishes Vāyu within the seasons.
8.3.3.[1] Then he lays down the *candasyā* bricks. The *candas* are cattle; the middle layer is the intermediate space; [he places them] in the intermediate space.
Thereby he places the animal; therefore animals have the intermediate space as their abode.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *candas* (metres):
the metres are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; cattle are the middle.
The middle layer is in the middle; thus he places that food in the center. He lays them down twelve by twelve.
The Jagatī meter indeed consists of twelve syllables; the Jagatī is cattle, and the intermediate space is the Jagatī.
The middle layer is in the intermediate space; thereby he places cattle therein. Therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode.
And again, as to why [he lays them] twelve by twelve:
the Jagatī meter consists of twelve syllables, and the Jagatī is cattle, for cattle are food.

The middle layer is the intermediate consciousness; he places that food in the middle. He places them immediately after the Prāṇabhṛts; he thus places food immediately after the vital breaths. Those [bricks] are higher; he thus places higher food after the vital breaths. 8.3.3. [5]

"Mā" means this world, for this world is as if measured; "pramā" means the intermediate space, for the intermediate space is as if measured from this world; "pratimā" means yonder world, for yonder world is indeed a reflection. "Candā" means... [the rest of the sentence is missing in the source].

For this is a counterpart in the world of the intermediate space; "asrīvayaś candaḥ" (the *canda* that flows forth)—food is what flows forth. Whatever food there is in these worlds, that is what flows forth (*asrīvaya*); and also, whatever food flows forth from these worlds, that is what flows forth. Now, therefore, he lays down the *candas* which are explicitly defined. 8.3.3. [6]
The *paṅkti* metre, the *uṣṇih* metre, the *bṛhatī* metre, the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *virāj* metre, the *gāyatrī* metre,
the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the *jagatī* metre— these are the [metres] explicitly defined, with the *virāj* as the eighth.
He lays down the *candas* (metres) with the words, "The earth is a *canda*, the atmosphere is a *canda*. Those *candas* which have these as their deities, those he thus lays down.
With the words, "Agni is the deity, Vāta is the deity," for these indeed are the deities that are the *candas*;
those he thus lays down. 8.3.3. [7]
He lays down both those that are defined and those that are undefined.
If he were to lay down all of them as defined, food would indeed come to an end; it would be exhausted. Therefore...
If all [bricks] were unexpressed (anirukta), food would have become something beyond perception; indeed, one would not even have seen it.
He lays down both expressed and unexpressed [bricks]; therefore, expressed food, while being eaten, is never exhausted. 8.3.3.
These, then, are they.
He lays down three sets of twelve; that makes thirty-six. The *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables.
This indeed is that *bṛhatī* which the gods then perceived as the third layer, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); of this very *bṛhatī*, the gods were the highest. 8.3.3 [9]
Moreover, as for why he lays down these bricks:
from Prajāpati, once he had become relaxed, all beings and all the quarters departed in different directions.

He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and those beings which departed from him are these very bricks. Thus, when he lays down these bricks, it is those very beings [that he restores] from him.
As he was departing from them, he now restores them to this [fire-altar].
Of these, those ten which he lays down first are the moon; they are ten in number, for the *daśākṣara* (ten-syllabled) [meter] consists of ten syllables.
The Virāj is food; the Virāj is food, and that is the moon. Now, as for the thirty-six [days] that follow, they are the half-months and the months:
twenty-four half-months and twelve months. The moon, indeed, is the year and all beings. 8.3.3. [12]
Where the gods fashioned him, there they placed all these beings within him;
in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places them within him. He lays those down immediately after the seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā), [that is], within the seasons.
He establishes all those beings. 8.3.4.[1] Now he lays down the *vālakhilyā* bricks.
The *vālakhilyās* are indeed the vital breaths; it is the vital breaths that he thus lays down. Those...
Or else, that which is called *vālakhilya* is that which remains unbroken between two fertile fields; they call that "waste" (*khila*).
Indeed, these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are unbroken by a mere hair's breadth (*vāla-mātra*); because they are unbroken by a mere hair's breadth, they are therefore called *vālakhilyās*.
He lays down seven [bricks] in front.
He places seven behind and seven in front; those which are these seven breaths in front, those he thus bestows upon him.
Now, as for those seven behind...
He thus makes these vital breaths the counterparts of those very vital breaths;
therefore, whatever food one eats with these [limbs], that he passes beyond by means of these. Furthermore, as to why he lays down seven bricks in front.
There are these seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in front:
the four parts of the forearms and upper arms, the head, the neck, and that which is above the navel is the seventh; for in every limb there is a vital breath.
These indeed are the seven vital breaths in front; he places them in this [body]. 8.3.4. [5]
Now, as for those seven behind:

there are indeed these seven vital breaths (prāṇas) behind—namely, the four thighs and knees, the two feet, and that which is below the navel as the seventh; for the vital breath is in every limb. These, indeed, are the seven.
Afterwards, he places those vital breaths within it:
"Thou art the head, the sovereign; thou art firm, the supporter; thou art the sustainer, the upholder; thou art the restrainer, the ruler; thou art the controller, the governess. (8.3.4.6)
"Thou art firm, the supporter," with these words he bestows upon him these very firm vital breaths.
And as to why he lays down the Vālakhilyas:
it was indeed the gods [who did so].

By means of the Vālakhilyā verses, they ascended these worlds—both upwards from here and downwards from there; in the same way, the sacrificer now ascends these worlds by means of the Vālakhilyā verses, both upwards from here and downwards from there.
"Thou art the head, the sovereign," with this he ascends this world.
With "Thou art firm, the supporter," he [establishes] the intermediate world;

with "Thou art the upholder, the sustainer," that [other] world; with "For life thee, for luster thee, for agriculture thee, for security thee," there are four [mantras]; cattle are four-footed, and cattle are food—by means of these four four-footed [mantras].

By means of these animals, this food, they established themselves in yonder world; in the same way, the sacrificer now establishes himself in yonder world by means of these four-footed animals and this food. 8.3.4.
[9] That [altar] is, as it were, an ascent in the opposite direction.

This earth is indeed the foundation; the gods returned to this foundation, and in the same way, the sacrificer now returns to this foundation. When he says, "The controller, the ruler," he ascends to yonder world.
With "Thou art the restrainer, for restraint," he [establishes] the intermediate world; with "Thou art the firm one, the supporter," this world.
With "Thee for food, thee for strength, thee for wealth, thee for prosperity"—these are four, and cattle are four-footed;
cattle are food. By means of these four four-footed cattle, by means of this food, [he establishes himself] in this world.
In the same way, the sacrificer establishes himself in this world by means of these four-footed animals and this food. Now, therefore, follows the consecration itself.

Those eleven bricks which he lays down—that first section (anuvāka)—is the intermediate region; that is the body. As to why there are eleven of them: the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the intermediate region is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. Now, those sixty [bricks] which follow are Vāyu, they are Prajāpati, they are Agni.
That sacrificer [is the body]. Now, those which he places in front are his head; they are ten in number, for there are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the vital breaths indeed [constitute the head].
He places [the bricks] on the eastern half; for this head is indeed in front.
Now, those which are to the south—those [bricks] are that part of him which is above the middle but below the head. And those which...
That which is above the foundation and below the middle—that is his [the altar's] foundations; they are on the north side. Now, as for those seven *vālakhilyā* bricks he lays down in front:
they are these very seven [breaths].

The vital breaths are in front; he thus places them in this [brick]. He lays them down so as not to be separated from these ten; he thereby places the vital breaths so as not to be separated from the head. Now, those seven which are behind—
Those very seven vital breaths which are behind, he places them in this [altar];
he lays them down immediately after these twelve, and thus he places the vital breaths within his own self without interruption.
This Vāyu Prajāpati is here, lying on all sides in this Traiṣṭubha mid-region; that which is the third...

He lays down the *citi*; he thus lays it down after having fashioned both Vāyu and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Then he lays down two *lokapṛṇā* bricks in this corner; the significance of those is explained above. He scatters loose earth (*purīṣa*); the significance of that is explained above. 8.4.1. [1] He lays down the fourth layer.
Having piled this third layer, the gods indeed ascended; for the third layer is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and having thus perfected the intermediate space, they ascended.
They said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek upwards from here! Thus they spoke.
While reflecting, they perceived this fourth layer: that which is above the intermediate space and below the sky;
for them, this world was, as it were, unstable and unestablished in their minds. They spoke to Brahmā.

"We shall place you here," they said. "What will become of me from that? "You yourself shall be the best among us. "So be it," they replied, and they placed the Brahman there. Therefore they say, "The Brahman is indeed the best among the gods. By means of this fourth layer, these two, heaven and earth, are supported; it is the Brahman.
The fourth layer indeed belongs to the Brahman; therefore they say, "Heaven and earth are supported by the Brahman. He lays down the *stomas*;
the *stomas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the vital breaths are the Brahman; thus he lays down the Brahman itself.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *stomas*...

The gods indeed said this to Prajāpati: "Let us place you here. He replied, "So be it. However, he did not say, "What will be mine from that? Whatever Prajāpati desired from the gods, they said, "What will be ours from that? Therefore, this is what a father [is].

Regarding the sons, they say, "What will come of that to us? And regarding the father, the sons say, "So be it. For thus did Prajāpati and the gods speak to one another in the beginning. He lays down the *stomas*;
the *stomas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and Prajāpati is indeed the vital breaths; it is Prajāpati himself whom he thus lays down. 8.4.1 [5]
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Stomas:

those very Rishis who saw this fourth layer were those who attained it by means of this essence; it is them that he now lays down. He lays down the Stomas, for the Stomas are indeed the vital breaths.
The vital breaths, indeed, are the *ṛṣis*; it is these very *ṛṣis* that he thus lays down. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *stomas*:
when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took him and departed; of him—
Then, having taken from him that which was above the navel and below the head, Vāyu departed after becoming the deities and the years; and he stood [there]. He said to him: 8.4.1.
[7] He said to him:
"Come to me; restore to me that by which you have departed from me. "What will be mine from that? "That part of my self shall belong to you as your own deity. "So be it.
Thereupon Vāyu restored this to him. 8.4.1 [8]
Now, as for these eighteen first [bricks]:
that is this self of his; and when he lays these down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this self of his. That is why he lays these down here.
He lays down the *stomas*. The *stomas* are indeed the vital breaths; Vāyu is indeed the vital breaths. It is Vāyu, therefore, that he thus lays down. He lays them down in front:
"The Swift, the Trivṛt"—he thus lays down that which is the Trivṛt *stoma*.

Now, as to why he says "the swift one" (āśu): for this is the swiftest of the *stomas*, and moreover, Vāyu is the swift one; he is the *trivṛt* and he moves through these three worlds. And as to why he says "the swift one": for he is the swiftest of all beings. Having become Vāyu, he stood in front; it is that very form he now deposits. 8.4.1 [10]
"The shining one, fifteenfold":

he thus lays down that very fifteenfold *stoma*; as to why he calls it "the shining one," the shining one is indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the thunderbolt is fifteenfold; moreover, the shining one is indeed the moon, which is fifteenfold.

And that [fortnight] is filled for fifteen days and diminished for fifteen days. As to why he says, "The shining one" (*bhānta*), it is because the moon shines; having become the moon, it stood on the south. He places that very form there. 8.4.1.
"The space, the seventeenfold."
He lays down that very seventeenfold *stoma*;

as to why he says "the void" (*vyoman*), Prajāpati is indeed the void, and Prajāpati is seventeenfold; moreover, the year is the void, and it is seventeenfold—its twelve months and five seasons. As to why he says "the void," for it is indeed the void.
The year; having become the year, it stood on the north. He places that very form there.
"The support, the twenty-onefold," he says;
he thus places that which is the twenty-onefold *stoma*. As to why he calls it "the support" (*dharuṇa*)—

Thus, the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is indeed the support (*dharuṇa*), and the twenty-onefold [stoma] is the foundation. Moreover, yonder sun is the support, the twenty-onefold; for him there are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun himself is the support, the twenty-onefold. As to why he calls it "the support": when this [sun] sets, then all this is supported.
Having become the Āditya, he stood behind; he thus lays down that very form.
Then he lays down the forms of the year:
"The rush, eighteen. (8.4.1.13)

That which is the eighteenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), that he lays down then; moreover, the year is indeed the "impulse" (*pratūrti*) consisting of eighteen parts: it has twelve months and five seasons, and the year itself is the eighteenfold impulse. As for why he calls it "impulse," it is because the year impels all beings forward.
He places that very form:
"Austerity is nineteen.
He thus places that which is the nineteenfold *stoma*; moreover, austerity is the year.

The nineteenth [brick] belongs to him; the twelve months, the six seasons, and the year itself are austerity (tapas), which is the nineteenth. As for why he says "austerity," it is because the year indeed heats (tapat) all beings; thus he lays down that very form. 8.4.1. [15] "The Overturner (abhīvarta) with twenty [bricks]."
He lays down that very *stoma* which consists of twenty; moreover, the *abhīvarta* is indeed the year consisting of twenty:

its twelve months, seven seasons, and the year itself is the *abhīvarta* consisting of twenty. As for why it is called the *abhīvarta*, it is because the year turns over (*abhivartate*) all beings; that is precisely why.
He lays down that brick with the formula:
"The twenty-two-fold [stoma] is splendor" (8.4.1.16).
He thus lays down that very twenty-two-fold stoma; moreover, it is indeed the year.
The twenty-second is *varcas* (splendor). Its [components] are the twelve months, the seven seasons, the two—day and night—and the year itself is the twenty-second *varcas*.
As for why he calls it *varcas*: the year is indeed the most splendid (*varcasvitama*) of all beings;
thus he places that very form. 8.4.1. [17]
"The twenty-third is the *sambharaṇa*. By this, he lays down that very twenty-three-fold hymn-form (*stoma*). Furthermore, the twenty-three-fold *sambharaṇa* is indeed the year:

its thirteen months, seven seasons, two—the day and night—and the year itself as the twenty-third *sambharaṇa*. As for why he calls it "the gathering" (*sambharaṇa*), it is because the year gathers together all beings.
Having been gathered together, he lays down that very form.
"The womb is the twenty-fourfold," he says;
he thus lays down that which is the twenty-fourfold *stoma*, and moreover, it is indeed the year.

The womb is the twenty-fourth; its twenty-four [parts] are the half-months. As for why he calls it the "womb" (*yoni*), the year is indeed the womb of all beings; he thus lays down that very form. "The embryos are the twenty-fifth," [he says].

He lays down that very twenty-five-fold hymn-form; moreover, the twenty-five-fold is indeed the womb, for there are twenty-four half-months and the year itself is the twenty-fifth womb. As to why he calls it "the wombs," it is because the year, having become the womb, becomes the thirteenth month.
"He enters the seasons; he thus lays down that very form.
(8.4.1.20) "The Triṇava is vigor. He thereby lays down that which is the Triṇava Stoma. As for why he calls it "vigor" (*ojas*), it is indeed *vāja* (strength).
Ojas is the twenty-sevenfold; moreover, the year is the twenty-sevenfold ojas. It has twenty-four half-months and two days and nights;

thus the year itself is the twenty-sevenfold ojas. As for why they call it "ojas," it is because the year is the most powerful (*ojasvitama*) of all beings; he thus lays down that very form. 8.4.1. [21]
"The Kratu is the thirty-onefold.
He thus lays down that which is the thirty-onefold Stoma. Moreover, the Kratu is indeed the year; it consists of twenty-four half-months, six seasons, and the year itself.
The thirty-first is *kratu* (will/resolve). As for why he says "kratu," it is because the year (*saṃvatsara*) indeed brings all beings into being;
he thus lays down that very form.
"The thirty-third is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). 8.4.1 [22]

That which is the Trayastrimsha Stoma, that he now lays down. As to why he calls it "the foundation" (pratiṣṭhā): the Trayastrimsha is indeed a foundation; moreover, the year is the foundation, and the Trayastrimsha is the year.
It consists of twenty-four half-months, six seasons, and two days and nights; the year itself is the foundation.
"The thirty-threefold is that which he calls 'the foundation' (pratiṣṭhā)," for the year is indeed the foundation of all beings;
it is that very form he deposits there.
"The summit of the radiant one (bradhnasya viṣṭapam) is the thirty-fourfold."

He lays down that which is this thirty-fourfold hymn-form (stoma). Moreover, the vault of the sun (bradhnasya viṣṭapam) is indeed the year; it consists of thirty-four parts: twenty-four half-months, seven seasons, and two—the day and night.
The year itself is the vault of the sun, the thirty-fourfold. As for why he says that...
"The summit of the radiant one"—the summit of the radiant one is indeed self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), and the thirty-fourfold [stoma] is self-sovereignty; he thus lays down that very form.
"The firmament, the thirty-sixfold"—thus [he says].

He lays down that very *ṣaṭtriṃśa* stoma. Moreover, the *nāka* is indeed the year; it consists of twenty-four half-months and twelve months. As to why he calls it *nāka*: for no one who has gone there finds any suffering (*aka*). Furthermore, the *nāka* is indeed the year; the year is the *nāka*.
The heavenly world is that very thing; he thus lays down that form.
"The turning-around is the forty-eightfold [stoma]"—he thereby lays down that which is the forty-eightfold stoma; moreover...

The year, indeed, is the revolving one (*vivarta*), consisting of forty-eight parts: twenty-six half-months, thirteen months, seven seasons, and two days and nights. As for why it is called "revolving" (*vivarta*): from the year all beings revolve;
thus he lays down that very form. 8.4.1 [26]

"The Dhartra is the Catuṣṭoma. He thus lays down that which is the Catuṣṭoma Stoma. As to why he calls it "Dhartra": the Dhartra is indeed a foundation, and the Catuṣṭoma is a foundation; moreover, Vāyu is indeed the Dhartra.

The Catuṣṭoma is praised with these four quarters. As to why he says "the support" (dhartra): the support is indeed a foundation, and Vāyu is the foundation of all beings; thus he lays down that very form.
He indeed lays down Vāyu first and Vāyu last; by means of Vāyu alone, he thereby [unifies] all these.
He encompasses the beings on both sides. 8.4.1.[27] Now, these eighteen bricks he lays down; they are two sets of threefold ones. The threefold is indeed breath;
Vāyu is breath, and this layer is Vāyu. 8.4.1.[28]
Or rather, why eighteen?

The year is indeed eighteenfold: twelve months and five seasons; the year itself is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is eighteenfold. Prajāpati is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—so great is this.
Having performed that much, he lays those down. Then he lays down the *spṛt* bricks.
For when this [part] of his own self had been restored, Prajāpati [recovered] all beings.
They became his embryos; while still within the womb, evil death seized them.
He said to the gods:
"Together with you, may I deliver all these beings from evil death."
"What will happen to us from that? he asked them. "Choose! he said to them. Some said, "Let there be a share for us.

Others said, "Let there be lordship for us. Having assigned a share to some and lordship to others, he delivered all beings from evil, from death; because he delivered (*aspṛṇot*) them, therefore it is called *spṛt*. In the same way, the sacrificer [does so].
Having assigned a portion to some and sovereignty to others, one delivers all beings from evil, from death;
therefore, in every case, the word "delivered" (*spṛtam*) follows.
8.4.2 [3] "Agni is your portion."

"The lordship of consecration (*dīkṣā*)," he said. Speech indeed is consecration; having made a portion for Agni, he established lordship over speech. "The *brahman* is protected by the threefold hymn-form (*trivṛt-stoma*)," he said. By means of the threefold hymn-form, he protected the *brahman* among creatures from evil, from death. 8.4.2 [4]
"You are the portion of Indra;

the overlordship of Viṣṇu"—having thus made a portion for Indra, he established overlordship for Viṣṇu. "The Kṣatra is won; the Pañcadaśa Stoma"—[he said this] regarding the Kṣatra among the subjects.
By means of the fifteenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), he delivered [them] from evil death.
"Thou art the portion of the Nṛcakṣases;
the sovereignty of Dhātṛ," [he says]. The Nṛcakṣases are indeed the gods; [it is] for the gods [that] the portion [is set aside].
Having established sovereignty, he made the *janitra* (the place of birth) secure with the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*). The *janitra* is indeed the people;
by means of the seventeenfold hymn-form, he freed the people from evil and death.
"Thou art the portion of Mitra."
