"Varuṇa’s lordship. Mitra is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), Varuṇa is the in-breath (*apāna*). Having assigned a portion to the out-breath, he made the in-breath his lordship. "Rain from heaven, the wind is released; the twenty-onefold hymn-form (*stoma*). By means of the twenty-onefold hymn-form, he delivered both rain and wind for living beings from evil, from death. 8.4.2 [7]
"You are the portion of the Vasus;
the sovereignty of the Rudras. Mitra is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and Varuṇa is the in-breath (*apāna*).
Having made the out-breath the portion, he made the in-breath the sovereignty. "The rain of heaven, the wind is won; the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*)," [he says], [referring to] the rain.
And by means of the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), he delivered the wind and the offspring from evil death.
"Thou art the portion of the Ādityas;
the lordship of the Maruts"—having thus assigned a portion to the Ādityas, [he assigned it] to the Maruts.

The embryos gained mastery; [with the thought] "the embryos are the twenty-fivefold hymn-form," he freed the embryos of offspring from evil, from death, by means of the twenty-fivefold hymn-form. 8.4.2.
[9] "Thou art the portion of Aditi."
"Pūṣan’s overlordship"—this earth is indeed Aditi; having made her a portion, he established Pūṣan's overlordship.
"Vital power has been won; the Triṇava Stoma"—by means of the Triṇava Stoma, he won for living beings vital power from evil, from death. 8.4.2 [10]
"Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ;

Bṛhaspati's overlordship. Having thus made a portion for the god Savitṛ, he established overlordship for Bṛhaspati. "The convergent quarters are secured; the Catuṣṭoma Stoma!"—thus [he secures] all the quarters.
By means of the fourfold *stoma*, he delivered the creatures from evil, from death.
"Thou art the portion of the *yavas*;
the overlordship of the *ayavas*. The *yavas* are indeed the bright fortnights (*pūrvapakṣas*), and the *ayavas* are the dark fortnights (*aparapakṣas*).
Or rather, he indeed took all this—both the young and the old—and having assigned a portion to the former fortnights, he established sovereignty over the latter fortnights.
Having rescued the creatures with the forty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), he delivered all creatures from evil, from death, by means of the forty-four-fold *stoma*. 8.4.2. [12]
"You are the portion of the Ṛbhus;

you are the overlordship of the Viśvedevas"—having thus made the portion for the Ṛbhus, he established the overlordship for the Viśvedevas. "The thirty-threefold hymn is what has come into being, what has been won"—thus [he assigned] all [the Stomas].

By means of the thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*), he [Prajāpati] delivered all beings from evil, death; in the same way, the sacrificer now delivers all beings from evil, death by means of the thirty-threefold hymn-form.
He lays down these ten bricks.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; Agni is the *virāj*. There are ten directions; the directions are Agni. There are ten vital breaths;
the vital breaths are Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—by that much alone he delivers all these beings from evil, from death. 8.4.2 [14]
Then he lays down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons that he lays down.
"Saha and Sahasya, the two winter seasons"—these are their names; it is by means of these very names that he lays them down.

There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months; he settles them once, and thus he makes it one season. Now, as to why he lays these down here: this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds. Of that [year],...

That which is above the intermediate space and below the sky—that is his fourth layer; that is his winter season. In that he places these two bricks here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this body of his; therefore he places these two here. 8.4.2. [16]
Moreover, as to why he lays these down here:
this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year. That part of him which is above the middle and below the head is this fourth layer; that is his winter.
The seasons are these; in that he lays these down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this body of his;
therefore he lays these down here.
Now he lays down the *sṛṣṭi* bricks.
Having freed all beings from evil and death, Prajāpati indeed desired: "May I create offspring; may I procreate. He spoke to the vital breaths (prāṇas). 8.4.3 [2]

"Let me procreate these creatures together with you. "With whom shall we sing praises? "With me and with you. "So be it. They sang praises with both the vital breaths and Prajāpati. Whatever the gods do, they do with a *stoma*; for the *stoma* is indeed the sacrifice; thus, they do it with the sacrifice itself.
Therefore, in all [the verses], the phrase "they praised, they praised" recurs.
Regarding the verse "With one [verse] they praised": the one is speech; with speech they then praised. "The creatures were established"—here, the creatures were indeed established.
"Prajāpati was the overlord"—Prajāpati was indeed the overlord here.
"They praised with three [verses]"—the vital breaths are indeed three: prāṇa, udāna, and vyāna; with these they then praised.
"Brahmā was created"—Brahmā was indeed created here; "Brahmaṇaspati was the overlord"—Brahmaṇaspati was indeed the overlord here.
"They praised with five"—[so it is said]. 8.4.3 [5]
Those very vital breaths, with mind as the fifth, praised with that [hymn].
"Beings were created," they said; indeed, beings were created here. "The Lord of Beings was the overlord," they said; indeed, the Lord of Beings was the overlord here. 8.4.3. [6]
"With seven they sang praises"—it was with these very seven vital breaths in the head that they then sang praises.
"The seven seers were created"—the seven seers were created here. "Dhātṛ was the overlord"—Dhātṛ was the overlord here. 8.4.3 [7]
‘They praised with nine’:
there are indeed nine vital breaths—seven in the head and two downward ones; with those very [breaths] they then praised.
‘The ancestors were created’: here the ancestors were created. ‘Aditi was the sovereign lady’: Aditi was here the sovereign lady. 8.4.3. [8]

"With eleven they sang praises"—the ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the self as the eleventh; with these very ones they sang praises. "The seasons were created"—the seasons were created here. "The seasonal deities were the overlords"—the seasonal deities were the overlords here. 8.4.3 [9]

"With thirteen they sang praise"—there are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*), two supports (*pratiṣṭhā*), and the self (*ātman*) is the thirteenth; with that very [thirteenfold] they sang praise. "The months were created"—the months were created here. "The year was the overlord"—the year [was the overlord].
He was the presiding lord.
"They praised with fifteen," [it is said].
There are ten fingers on the hands, four arms and forearms, and that which is above...
"The fifteenth was from the navel; with that they praised. 'The Kṣatra was created,' they said; thus the Kṣatra was created here.
'Indra was the overlord,' they said; thus Indra was the overlord here.
(8.4.3)[11] "They praised with seventeen [verses]," it is said.

There are ten toes, four thighs and knees, and two feet; that which is below the navel is the seventeenth. With that they praised. "Domestic animals were created," they said; thus domestic animals were created here. "Bṛhaspati was the overlord," they said; Bṛhaspati was the overlord here. 8.4.3 [12]
"With nine and ten they praised.
There are ten fingers on the hand and nine vital breaths; with those very [limbs] they praised.
"Let the Śūdra and the Ārya be released"—the Śūdra and the Ārya were released here. "Let Day and Night be the two consorts"—Day and Night [were the consorts].
In this case, there were two presiding wives (adhipatnī).
"They praised with twenty-one," [it is said];
there are ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and the self is the twenty-first—by that very [number].

They praised with twenty-three; single-hoofed animals were created—single-hoofed animals were created here; Varuṇa was the overlord—Varuṇa was the overlord here. 8.4.3.[14] "They praised with twenty-three."

The ten fingers of the hand, the ten toes of the foot, the two feet as supports, and the self as the twenty-third—with that they then praised. "Small animals were created," they said; thus small animals were created here.
"Pūṣan was the overlord," they said; Pūṣan was indeed the overlord. 8.4.3 [15]
"With twenty-five they praised," [it is said].
There are ten fingers on the hands, ten on the feet, four limbs, and the self as the twenty-fifth; with that very thing they praised. "Wild animals were created"—wild animals were created here.
"Vāyu was the overlord"—meaning Vāyu was the overlord here.
"They praised with twenty-seven":
ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, four limbs, and two supports.
The self was the twenty-seventh; with that very [self], they praised it, saying: "Heaven and earth went apart. Here heaven and earth went apart.

"The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas followed after them," they said; the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas followed after them here. "They were the overlords," they said; they indeed were the overlords here. 8.4.3. [17]
"With twenty-nine they praised," [it is said].

There are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, and nine vital breaths; with these very [limbs] they then praised. "The trees were created," [it is said]; the trees were created here. "Soma was the overlord," [it is said].
Soma was the presiding deity here.
"They praised with thirty-one"—
there are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, and ten vital breaths.
With the self as the thirty-first, they praised with that very [verse]: "The creatures were created. Thus, the creatures were created here.
"The Yavas and Ayavas were the overlords," they said; the bright and dark fortnights were indeed the overlords here.
"They praised with thirty-three," it is said.

There are ten fingers, ten toes, ten vital breaths, two supports, and the self as the thirty-third; with that very [self] they praised. "The beings were stilled," they said; for all beings were stilled therein. Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin was the overlord; thus it was Prajāpati.
Parameṣṭhin was the overlord here.
Now, these bricks he lays down are seventeen; for Prajāpati, the year, is seventeenfold, and he is the progenitor.
Thus, by means of this seventeenfold Prajāpati, the year, the progenitor, these creatures [are produced].

What he generated, he created; and because he created them, they are called *sṛṣṭis*. Having created those *sṛṣṭis*, he caused them to enter into himself. In the very same way, the sacrificer, by means of this seventeenfold year as Prajāpati, generates these creatures; having generated them, he causes them to enter into himself.
By the region of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; for the two *retaḥsic*s are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle. Thus, he causes these offspring to enter him from the very middle.
He lays them down on all sides; thus, he causes these offspring to enter him from every side. 8.4.4. Now, therefore, follows the sequence of the procedure.

He places one containing the *trivṛt* in front, one containing the *ekaviṃśa* behind, one containing the *pañcadaśa* to the south, and one containing the *saptadaśa* to the north. This, indeed, is Prajāpati.

When the [brick] possessed of the *trivṛt* had been laid down, and when the one possessed of the *pañcadaśa* was about to be laid down, Death sat there [thinking], "He will lay this down from here; I shall seize him there. He (the sacrificer) saw him;
having perceived him and moved around him, he laid down the one possessed of the *ekaviṃśa*, then the one possessed of the *ekaviṃśa*.
Death approached; he took up a fifteen-fold [stoma]; death approached;
he took up a seventeen-fold [stoma]. Right there he overcame death, right there he confounded it. In the very same way, the sacrificer right here overcomes all evils, right here he confounds them.
It causes delusion. 8.4.4.[3] Now, the subsequent ones:
upon a brick containing the *trivṛt* [stoma], she places one containing the *trivṛt*; upon one containing the *ekaviṃśa*, she places one containing the *ekaviṃśa*.

In the fifteenfold [stoma] he lays down the seventeenfold, and in the seventeenfold the fifteenfold. Because he thus lays them down crosswise, they are therefore called *akṣṇayāstomīyā*. Furthermore, because these *stomas* are otherwise than in their regular sequence, for that reason also they are called *akṣṇayāstomīyā*. Moreover, the gods laid them down in this way, whereas the Asuras did otherwise; therefore, the gods [prevailed].
His enemies become breathless; he becomes superior by his own self, and his hateful rival becomes defeated—he who knows thus.
This Agni is indeed the sacrificial animal.
He is here entirely and completely consecrated; his two heads are the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa* [stomas].

In that there are two bricks containing the *trivṛt* [stoma], for the head is threefold; there are two [of them], for the head consists of two skull-bones (*kapāla*). He places them on the eastern half, for this head is in front. The two bricks containing the *ekaviṃśa* [stoma] are the foundation.
As for why there are two [bricks] containing twenty-one, it is because the twenty-one-fold is a foundation;
there are two of them because a foundation is a pair. He lays them down behind, for this foundation is behind. The two containing fifteen are the arms.
As for the fact that there are two [bricks] containing the *pañcadaśa* [stoma]: the arms are indeed *pañcadaśa*;
they are two, for these two arms are two; he places them on the sides, for these two arms are on the sides.
The two [bricks] containing the *saptadaśa* [stoma] are food.

As to why there are two bricks containing the word "seventeen," it is because food is seventeenfold; and as to why there are two, it is because food has two syllables. He places them immediately adjacent to the two bricks containing the word "fifteen"; thus he places food immediately adjacent to the two arms on the outside.
There are two [bricks] consisting of fifteen, and two consisting of seventeen on either side of them; with these two arms, he thus encompasses the food.
Then, as for those which he places in the middle:
He places that self within the range of the two *retaḥsic* bricks.

For the two *retaḥsic*s are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle; for this self is in the middle. He places it on every side, for this self is on every side. Now, as for what is other than this, it is redundant; and whatever among the gods is redundant, those are the *chandas* meters.
Now, those *candāṃsi* (verses) are the cattle; those cattle are the auspicious marks (*puṇyā lakṣmyaḥ*); and those auspicious marks are yonder sun. He is to their south.
Some, indeed, place these [bricks] without an interval from the two [verses] containing the word "trivṛt."

As for those who say, "The fourteen [bricks] are the jaws and the six are the tongue," one should not do so; they leave a deficiency. One should rather place the latter jaws upon the former jaws, just as one places the latter tongue upon the former tongue.
One should place the tongue upon it; for that which is the head is indeed those two jaws and that tongue.
8.4.4.[10] Now, some place these in the intermediate space; [they say] "The sun yonder is these bricks," and thus they place yonder sun in this [space].
"One should not do so [thinking], 'We place it in the direction,' for those are indeed other rites by which one places this here.
Some, however, place them on the south side,
thinking, "We place these auspicious marks on the south side."

Therefore, they call one who has a mark on the right side "one of auspicious marks," while for a woman it is on the left, for the woman’s abode is on the left. However, he should actually lay them down in front; where the head is, there are the jaws and the tongue. Thus he places this auspicious mark in the mouth; therefore, it is on the face of one who has it.
He possesses that mark; therefore they call him "one of meritorious fortune" (puṇyalakṣmīka).
This is the Brahma-piling:
because they piled up the Brahman, it is therefore called the Brahma-piling.
It is the Prajāpati-layer because they laid down Prajāpati; therefore it is the Prajāpati-layer.
It is the Ṛṣi-layer because they laid down the Ṛṣis; therefore it is the Ṛṣi-layer. It is the Vāyu-layer because they laid down Vāyu;
therefore it is the Vāyu-layer. It is the Stoma-layer because they laid down the Stomas; therefore it is the Stoma-layer. That [is] she.

The Prāṇaciti is so called because they piled it with the vital breaths; therefore, it is the Prāṇaciti. Whatever one may know, by that very knowledge this piling of his becomes possessed of a lineage and possessed of kinship. Then he piles two Lokampṛṇā bricks in that corner; their significance is above that. He scatters loose soil (purīṣa); its significance is above that. 8.5.1. [1]
He lays down the fifth layer.
Indeed, having built the fourth layer, the gods ascended; they prepared that which is above the intermediate space and below the sky, and having prepared it, they ascended. 8.5.1.2.
They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)! or rather, "Seek [something] from here upwards!
While meditating, they perceived the sky itself as the Virāj, the fifth layer. This world appeared pleasing to them.
They desired it.
"Let us make this world free from rivals and free from affliction," they said.
"Consider how we may make this world free from rivals and free from affliction," they said.
"Meditate! they said; by this they meant, "Seek a layer (citi). "Seek it so that... they said.
"Let us make the world free from rivals and free from affliction," they thought.
Reflecting thus, they saw these *asapatnā* bricks; they laid them down, and by means of them, this—
They made this world free from rivals and free from affliction;

because they made this world free from rivals and free from affliction by means of these [bricks], therefore these are called *asapatnāḥ*. In the same way, when the sacrificer lays these down, he makes this very world free from rivals and free from affliction. He lays them down on all sides.

In every respect, he thus makes this world free from rivals and free from affliction; he places them in the higher half, and thus he makes this entire world free from rivals and free from affliction. 8.5.1.
[5] Now he lays down the Virāj bricks.

This indeed is that Virāj which the gods saw as the fifth layer, the Virāj; he lays them down ten by ten, for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and this layer is the Virāj. He lays them down on all sides;
for he who shines in only one direction does not truly shine, but he who shines in all directions truly shines.
He alone shines forth.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down these *asapatnā* bricks:
when this part of his own self had been restored, Prajāpati shone forth.
He was pursued on all sides by evil; he saw these *asapatnā* bricks and laid them down.
By means of them, he struck away that evil. Evil, indeed, is the rival (*sapatna*). Because he struck away the evil, the rival, by means of these, they are therefore called *asapatnā*. 8.5.1. [7]

This very thing is done now which the gods did; that evil does not approach this person. But when he performs this, it is with the thought, "I shall do what the gods did," and furthermore, [it serves] against whatever evil there may be.

By these [bricks], he strikes away his rival; because he strikes away evil, the rival, by means of these, they are called *asapatnāḥ* (rival-less). He lays them down on all sides; thus he strikes away evil, the rival, from every side. He lays them down in the further half; thus he strikes away evil, the rival, from the very extremity of his self. 8.5.1. [8]

He places it in front with the words, "O Agni, drive away our born enemies," for as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. Then he places it behind with the words, "By force, drive away our born enemies," for as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. 8.5.1. [9]
That which was in front was Agni; that which was behind was Agni. By means of Agni itself, they thus drove away evil from the front by means of Agni.
Afterwards, in the same way, the sacrificer repels evil from the front by means of Agni and from behind by means of Agni. Then, from the south:
"The *ṣoḍaśī* chant, vigor, wealth"—this [verse] indeed consists of eleven syllables.

The Triṣṭubh is connected with the Triṣṭubh; the intermediate space is [connected with] the Triṣṭubh, and there are four quarters. This very [stoma] is the fifteenfold thunderbolt; that Aditya yonder is its sixteenth part, the bearer of the thunderbolt.
With this fifteenfold thunderbolt, this Triṣṭubh, he (the sacrificer) struck away evil from the south; in the same way, the sacrificer now [strikes it away] by means of this.
With this fifteenfold vajra, with this triṣṭubh metre, he repels evil from the south. 8.5.1.[11] Now, from the north:
"The forty-fourfold stoma, splendor, wealth"—for there are indeed forty-four syllables [in the jagatī].

The Triṣṭubh is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh, and the thunderbolt is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. With this forty-four-syllable thunderbolt and with this Triṣṭubh, he (the sacrificer) struck away evil from the north.
In the very same way, the sacrificer now strikes away evil from the north with this forty-four-syllable thunderbolt and with this Triṣṭubh. 8.5.1. [12]
Then, in the middle:
"Thou art the soil of Agni. The fourth layer is indeed the Brahman, and Agni is the Brahman; that which is the fifth layer is like its soil. Its significance has already been explained. 8.5.1. [13]
He lays it down across towards the east.
For by this [brick], Prajāpati cut off the root of evil; in the same way, he now cuts off the root of evil with this one on the south side.
For the thunderbolt is raised from the south; he thus makes that space for its upward raising within the southern quarter. That which is in front is the out-breath (*prāṇa*).
That which is the out-breathing (*apāna*) behind is the same as the in-breathing (*prāṇa*);

by means of that very in-breathing he struck away evil from the front, and by means of the out-breathing from behind. In the same way, the sacrificer now strikes away evil from the front by means of the in-breathing, and from behind by means of the out-breathing. 8.5.1. [15]
Then those two which were on both sides [became] his two arms. Whatever evil was of him on both sides, he struck it away with his two arms;
in the very same way, whatever evil belongs to this sacrificer on both sides, he strikes it away with his two arms alone. 8.5.1. [16]
The *anna* (food) brick is the one containing soil. Whatever evil was above him, he drove that away by means of food;
in the same way, the sacrificer now drives away whatever evil is above him by means of food alone. 8.5.1. [17]
Indeed, when one who knows this breathes out, he strikes away with that whatever evil is before him;
and when he breathes in, he strikes away with that whatever is behind him; and when he performs action with his two arms, he strikes away with that whatever is on both sides.
Then, by the food he eats, he [removes that evil]. Indeed, one who knows this always removes evil even while sleeping;
therefore, one should not mention the evil of one who knows this, lest one should incur his evil. 8.5.2. Then he lays down the *candasyā* bricks.

Prajāpati, having freed himself from evil and death, desired food; therefore, even one who is suffering, having become better off, desires food. They place their hope in him, saying, "He desires food; he will live. For him, the gods prepared this food.
These meters bestowed [them]; for the meters are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; they bestowed them upon him. Because they bestowed them upon him, therefore they are called *candāṃsi*.
He lays them down ten by ten.
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is indeed all food. Thus, he bestows upon him this entire food in its completeness. He places it on all sides;
verily, he bestows upon him this entire food from every side. 8.5.2 [3]
"Evācchandaḥ"—this world is indeed *evācchandaḥ*; "varivacchandaḥ"—the intermediate space is indeed *varivacchandaḥ*;
"śambhūcchandaḥ"—the sky is indeed *śambhūcchandaḥ*; "paribhūcchandaḥ"—the quarters are indeed *paribhūcchandaḥ*.
The *ācaccanda* is food; the *manaścanda* is Prajāpati;
the *vyacaścanda* is yonder sun; and the *sindhuścanda*—thus [they say]. 8.5.2.[4]
The *sindhu* metre is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the *samudra* metre is the mind (*manas*). The *sarira* metre is speech (*vāc*); the *kakubh* metre is the vital breath;
the *trikakubh* metre is the upward breath (*udāna*). The *kāvya* metre is the triple Veda (*trayī*).

The Vidyā is the *canda*; the *aṅkuṣa* is the *canda*, for water indeed is the *aṅkuṣa-canda*. The *akṣarapaṅkti* is the *canda*; this world indeed is the *akṣarapaṅkti-canda*. The *padapaṅkti* is the *canda*; this world indeed is the *padapaṅkti-canda*. The *viṣṭārapaṅkti* is the *canda*; the quarters indeed are the *viṣṭārapaṅkti-canda*. The razor...

"Bhrajaś-canda" (the blazing one, the radiant)—this indeed is the sun, the razor, the blazing one, the radiant. "Ācaccanda" (the approaching radiant one) and "pracaccanda" (the advancing radiant one)—food indeed is the approaching radiant one, food is the advancing radiant one. "Saṃyaccanda" (the unifying radiant one).

"Night is indeed the *saṃyac-candas*, 'the unifying metre'; day is indeed the *viyac-candas*, 'the separating metre'. The *bṛhat-candas*, 'the great metre', is yonder world; the *rathantara-candas*, 'the chariot-metre', is this world.
The *nikāya-candas*, 'the gathering metre', is the wind; the *vivadha-candas*, 'the carrying-yoke metre', is the intermediate space."

“*Vivadha* is a *chandas*, *giraś-candas* is a *chandas*”—food indeed is *giraś-candas*; “*bhrajaś-candas* is a *chandas*”—fire indeed is *bhrajaś-candas*; “*saṃstuc-candas*, *anuṣṭubh-candas* is a *chandas*”—speech indeed is *saṃstuc-candas*, speech is *anuṣṭubh-candas*; “*evas-candas*, *varivas-candas* is a *chandas*”—the significance of this has been explained. 8.5.2. [6]
"Vayas-candas": food indeed is the *vayas*-meter; "vayaskṛt-candas": Agni indeed is the *vayaskṛt*-meter;
"viṣpardhās-candas": yonder world indeed is the *viṣpardhās*-meter; "viśālam-candas": this world indeed is the *viśālam*-meter.

The *candas* are: *viśālam candaḥ*, *cadiścandaḥ*; *cadiḥ* is indeed the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), and *candaḥ*; *dūrohaṇam candaḥ*; *dūrohaṇa* is indeed yonder sun (*āditya*), and *candaḥ*; *tandram candaḥ*; *tandra* is indeed the *paṅkti* [meter], and *candaḥ*; *aṅkāṅkam candaḥ*; *aṅkāṅka* is indeed the waters, and *candaḥ*. 8.5.2. [7]
Now, those which he lays down in front:
of these, the first is the out-breath (prāṇa),
the second the through-breath (vyāna), the third the up-breath (udāna), the fourth the up-breath, the fifth the through-breath, the sixth the out-breath, and the seventh the out-breath.

The Vyāna is the eighth, the Udāna the ninth, and the sacrificer himself is the tenth here. This very sacrificer is established and supported upon this Virāj, consisting of breath; he lays down [the bricks] directed both hitherward and thitherward, and therefore these vital breaths move both hitherward and thitherward. 8.5.2. [8]
Now, as for those on the south:

Agni is the first of them, Vāyu the second, Āditya the third, Āditya the fourth, Vāyu the fifth, Agni the sixth, Agni the seventh, Vāyu the eighth, Āditya the ninth; here, the sacrificer himself is [the tenth].
This tenth [brick] is that very sacrificer; established upon this Virāj, which consists of the deities, he lays down both those directed hitherward and those directed awayward.
Therefore, these gods are both hitherward and awayward.
Now, as for those which are behind...
This world is their first; the intermediate space is the second; the sky is the third; the sky is the fourth; the intermediate space is the fifth; this world is the sixth; this world is the seventh;
the intermediate space is the eighth; the sky is the ninth; the sacrificer himself is the tenth here—he is indeed this sacrificer.
Upon this Virāj, which consists of the worlds, he establishes and rests; and upon it he lays down both those that are directed hitherward and those that are directed awayward.
Therefore these worlds are both directed hitherward and directed awayward. Now, as for those [bricks] on the north side—
Summer is their first, the rainy season the second,
winter the third, winter the fourth, the rainy season the fifth, summer the sixth, summer the seventh,
the rainy season the eighth, winter the ninth, and the sacrificer himself is the tenth here. This very sacrificer [is established] in this [tenth].

The Virāj is supported by and established upon the Seasonal bricks; he lays down both those directed hitherward and those directed thitherward, and therefore these seasons are both hitherward and thitherward. Then, once again—
Those which he places in front are the vital breaths; they are ten in number, for there are indeed ten vital breaths.
He places them in the eastern half, for these vital breaths are indeed in the front.
Now, those which [he places] on the south—
These are those deities: Agni and the Earth, Vāyu and the Intermediate Space, Āditya and the Sky, the Moon and the Stars, as well as Food and Water.
Now, those that are behind:
Those are the four quarters, the four intermediate quarters, the zenith, and this [earth]. 8.5.2.[14] Now, those that are on the north:
they are the months—two of spring, two of summer, two of the rainy season, and two of autumn.
There are two winter months and two [spring months].
8.5.2.[15] Now again: that which is the first decade is this world; that which is the second is the intermediate space; and that which is the third—

By the first decade they ascended this very world, by the second the intermediate space, and by the third the sky; in the same way, the sacrificer now ascends this very world by the first decade, the intermediate space by the second, and the sky by the third. 8.5.2 [16]
That is like a tree growing away from its base;
this earth, indeed, is the foundation. The gods returned to this foundation, and in the same way, the sacrificer now returns to this foundation. Then...

That which is the highest tenfold set is this world; therefore, just as it begins with the first tenfold set, so it is with the highest, for these two tenfold sets are the same, being this very world. These, indeed, are forty bricks and forty sacrificial formulas.
"Eighty is food, eighty is that. Whatever he says here, having made that into food and eighty, he gives it to him;
thereby he gratifies him.
8.5.3.[1] Now he lays down the *stomabhāga* bricks.
This, indeed, is the food of Prajāpati; Indra set his mind upon it. He desired to depart from him, and Prajāpati said to him: "Why do you depart? Why do you leave me? He replied:
"Give me the essence of this food; enter into me together with that. [Prajāpati said: "So be it. To him, he gave the essence of that food.
He entered into him together with that expiation. 8.5.3.[2] That which was Prajāpati is this very Agni who is being built up; and that which was food are these Chandasyā bricks.
Now, that which is the essence of food—these are the *stomabhāgās*. And he who is Indra is yonder sun;
he is indeed this very *stoma*, for whatever they praise with, they praise him alone by that means.
He gave this portion to that *stoma*; because he gave this portion to that *stoma*, therefore they are called *stomabhāgās*. 8.5.3. [3]

"By the ray, quicken truth with truth!"—the ray is indeed food; having thus joined this [food] and its essence, he causes it to enter into himself. "By the impulse, quicken dharma with dharma!"—the impulse is indeed food.
Having joined together this [breath] and its essence, he offers it to himself, saying, "Anviti! Do thou quicken heaven day by day.
*Anviti* is indeed food; food is *anviti*. Having joined together this [breath] and its essence, he offers it to himself.
Whatever he says therein, having joined together that and its essence, he offers it to himself, saying, "O Food, do thou quicken with food! Thou art food for such-and-such a one."
"May the lord of thee, O strength, quicken strength"—thus they are laid down in threefold fashion, for food is indeed threefold.
And as to why he lays down the *stomabhāga* bricks:
the gods, having built the *virāj* layer, ascended it.
When they said, "Meditate! it was indeed this they meant: "Seek a layer!
While meditating, they beheld the vaulted world of heaven; they laid it down. That which is that vaulted world of heaven—these are the *stomabhāgā* bricks.
Thus, when he lays these down, he lays down the vaulted world of heaven. 8.5.3. [5]
Of those [verses], the first three are this world; the second are the intermediate space; the third are the sky.
Those that are the fourth are the eastern direction; those that are the fifth are the southern direction; those that are the sixth are the western direction.
The seventh is the northern one.
These, then, are those twenty-one bricks: these worlds and the quarters. For these worlds and the quarters are the foundation;
these worlds and the quarters are the twenty-one. Therefore they say, "The twenty-one is the foundation."
Now, as for those eight bricks that remain over:

the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman; thus, that which is the Brahman is this very thing, namely, that orb which shines there. This [Brahman] rests upon that twenty-first [brick].
Established, it shines; therefore, it does not fall away. 8.5.3.

[8] Now, some place the thirtieth brick with the formula, "The glory of the dress, quicken the kṣatra for the kṣatra," saying, "The Virāj has thirty syllables; this layer is the Virāj. One should not do so; they [go] beyond.

They chant the perfection of the twenty-one-fold stoma, and then the perfection of the Gāyatrī. This is indeed Indra’s world; for this Virāj is deficient by one syllable. For Indra, in his own world, they thus make the hating enemy rise up against them, and they drive Indra away from Indra’s world. Indeed, the sacrificer is Indra in his own sacrifice; it is for the sacrificer that they [act].
They make the hating rival who seeks to oppose him in the world of the sacrificer; they drive the sacrificer away from the world of the sacrificer.
This very fire which they bring here is the sacrificer by his own abode, and he indeed is the thirtieth here. 8.5.4. [1]
He lays them down at the limit of the Aṣāḍhā brick.
The Aṣāḍhā is speech, and this is the essence; he thus places the essence in speech.
Therefore, among all the limbs, it is by means of speech alone that one discerns the essence of food. 8.5.4 [2]
Furthermore, regarding the Aṣāḍhā brick:
this earth is indeed Aṣāḍhā, and the Stomabhāgas are yonder sun; he thus establishes yonder sun upon this earth as its foundation. 8.5.4 [3]
Furthermore, regarding the Aṣāḍhā brick:
this earth, indeed, is the Aṣāḍhā, and the Stomabhāgas are the heart. He thus places that heart and mind in her;
therefore, one perceives with the heart and mind through her. He lays them down on all sides.

He places his heart and mind upon it from every side; therefore, he perceives with his heart and mind from every side through this [mark]. Moreover, these are auspicious marks (*lakṣmyaḥ*); he places them all around himself. Therefore, they call one who has a mark on every side "one possessed of auspicious marks. 8.5.4. [4]
Then he covers them with loose soil (*purīṣa*).
The loose soil is indeed food, and this [fire-altar] is its essence; he thus conceals that essence from view.
Therefore, the essence of food is, as it were, hidden. 8.5.4[5]
Furthermore, as to why it is with *purīṣa*:
*purīṣa* is indeed food, and this [fire] is the essence; thus he connects and joins together both the food and its essence. 8.5.4. [6]
Moreover, as for the fact that it is with loose earth (purīṣa): the Stomabhāgas are indeed the heart, and the loose earth is the pericardium; he thus covers the heart with the pericardium. 8.5.4 [7]
And as to why it is with the loose soil (purīṣa):
this Agni is the year; he thus divides him by means of the layers and the loose soil.
Now, those which are the first four layers are the four seasons; then, having laid down the Stomabhāga bricks, he puts down the loose soil.
He scatters [the seeds]; that is the fifth layer, that is the fifth season.
Regarding this, they say: "Since the other layers end with the *lokampṛṇā* bricks, why does he not place a *lokampṛṇā* here? What is the *lokampṛṇā* here?
Indeed, yonder sun is the *lokampṛṇā*, and this very layer is it; thus, this layer is itself a self-sufficient *lokampṛṇā*. Then...
That which is above this, up to the loose soil (purīṣa), is the sixth layer; that is the sixth season. 8.5.4.
[9] Then he scatters the loose soil.
Therein he also places the Vikarṇī brick and [scatters] chips of gold.

He sprinkles [the earth] and places fuel upon the fire; that is the seventh layer, that is the seventh season. Indeed, those [bricks] are only six, for the *vikarṇī* and the *svayamātṛṇā* belong to the sixth layer itself.
But indeed, there are only five layers.
In the other layers he scatters loose soil with a *yajus* formula, but here he does so silently; therefore this is not a layer.
Furthermore, the other layers end with *lokampṛṇā* bricks, but here he does not place a *lokampṛṇā*; therefore this also is not a layer. 8.5.4. [12]

But indeed, there are only three: this world is the first layer, and the sky is the last; and those which are these three [intermediate layers] are the intermediate space. Now, that intermediate space is, as it were, one; thus they are three, and thus five.
Thus there are six; [then he lays down] seven.
8.6.1.[1] He lays down the *nākasad* bricks.
The gods are indeed the *nākasads*; here this entire Agni has been prepared, and it is he who is here.
Nāka is the heavenly world; in it the gods sat down. Because the gods sat down in that Nāka, the heavenly world, they are therefore called the "Nākasads" (those who sit on the firmament).
In the same way, when the sacrificer lays these bricks down, he sits down in that very Nāka, the heavenly world. 8.6.1. [2]
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *nākasad* bricks:
the gods indeed saw this vault, this heavenly world;
they were these *stomabhāga* formulas, and they said, "Find out how we may sit upon this vault, in this heavenly world. They...
When they said, "Be mindful," they were indeed saying, "Seek a layer; seek it so that we may sit upon this vault in the heavenly world. As they were thus reflecting, 8.6.1 [3].
They saw these bricks; they laid them down as the *nākasads*. By means of them, they settled upon that firmament, in the heavenly world.

Because they settled upon that firmament, in the heavenly world, by means of them, therefore these are called *nākasads*. In the very same way, when the sacrificer lays these down, he settles him upon this very firmament, in the heavenly world.
It settles. He places them in the quarters.
The quarters are indeed that firmament, the heavenly world; thus he places them in the heavenly world itself.

He sets them down at the juncture of the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). The seasonal bricks are the year; the year is the heavenly world. Thus, he places them in that very world, the heaven. Within the *stomabhāga* formula—this indeed is the firmament (*nāka*), the heavenly world—he thereby establishes them therein. 8.6.1. [5]
He places it in front:

"The queenly one is the eastern quarter," for this eastern quarter is indeed named the Queenly; "the Vasus are the gods, the overlords," for the Vasus are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter; "Agni [is the lord] of missiles."

"The upholder"—for Agni indeed is the upholder here of the attackers; "may the threefold Stoma rest upon the earth"—for by means of the threefold Stoma this [earth] rests upon the earth; "may the Ājya-uktha prop it for steadiness"—for by means of the Ājya-uktha this [earth] is propped upon the earth for steadiness; "may the Rathantara Sāman for stability in the atmosphere."

It is established in the intermediate space by means of the Rathantara Sāman. "The Ṛṣis, the first-born among the gods, [establish] thee"—the Ṛṣis are indeed the vital breaths, for that Brahman is the first-born. "May they expand with the measure and the width of heaven"—that is to say, may they expand with as much width as there is in heaven. "And this Vidhartṛ and the Adhipati"—these two are Speech and Mind.

"And may both Mind and Speech sustain all this; may they, being in full agreement, establish you and the sacrificer upon the back of the firmament, in the heavenly world"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. 8.6.1 [6] Then, on the south side.
"Thou art Virāj, the southern quarter," for this southern quarter is indeed named Virāj;

"the Rudras are the gods who are its overlords," for the Rudras are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter; "Indra is the repeller of missiles," for Indra indeed is here the repeller of missiles; "the Pañcadaśa-stoma [is thine] upon the earth."
"May she rest," he says; for by means of the fifteenfold *stoma*, she rests upon the earth. "May the *prauga* hymn support her for the sake of non-distress," he says;

for by means of the *prauga* hymn, she is supported upon the earth for the sake of non-distress. "May the *bṛhat* sāman establish her in the intermediate space for the sake of stability," he says; for by means of the *bṛhat* sāman, she is established in the intermediate space. "O seers, you [support] her..."
"Born first among the gods"—the significance of this has already been explained. 8.6.1 [7].
Now, behind:
"Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), the western quarter. For this western quarter is indeed named the Sovereign; its deities are the Ādityas.

"The overlords"—the Ādityas are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter; "Varuṇa, the repeller of missiles"—for Varuṇa is indeed the repeller of missiles here; "May the seventeenfold Stoma support you on earth"—for by means of the seventeenfold Stoma she is supported on earth; "The Marutvatīya hymn for stability."

"May he support [the earth] with the Marutvatīya-uktha," for by this uktha she is supported upon the earth so that she may not waver; "with the Vairūpa-sāman for stability in the intermediate space," for by the Vairūpa-sāman she is established in the intermediate space; "O first-born seers among the gods..."—the significance of this has already been explained. 8.6.1. [8]
Then, from the north: "Svarāj is this northern quarter"—for this northern quarter is indeed named Svarāj;

"the Maruts are the gods who are its overlords"—for the Maruts are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter; "Soma is the repeller of missiles"—for Soma indeed is here the repeller of missiles; "the twenty-one-fold Stoma [is established] upon the earth."

"May she rest upon it"—with the twenty-onefold *stoma*, she is indeed supported upon the earth. "May the *niṣkevalya* hymn stabilize her for the sake of non-distress"—with the *niṣkevalya* hymn, she is indeed stabilized upon the earth for the sake of non-distress. "O King, may the *sāman* Vairāja establish you"—with the *sāman* Vairāja, she is established in the intermediate space. "The seers [support] you..."
"Born first among the gods"—the significance of this has already been explained.
Now, in the middle:
"Thou art the sovereign lady, the great quarter. For this great quarter is indeed named the Sovereign Lady (*adhipatnī*). All these...

"The gods are the overlords"—for all the gods are indeed the overlords of this quarter; "Bṛhaspati is the warder-off of missiles"—for Bṛhaspati indeed is here the warder-off of missiles; "May the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas support you on earth"—for by means of these two Stomas, the Triṇava and the Trayastriṃśa, she is supported on earth.

"May the Vaiśvadeva and Agnimāruta hymns support [the earth] so that it does not waver"—by means of these two hymns, the Vaiśvadeva and Agnimāruta, she is supported upon the earth so that she does not waver. "The Śākvara and Raivata Sāmans for stability in the intermediate space"—by means of these two Sāmans, the Śākvara and Raivata, she is established in the intermediate space. "The Ṛṣis you..."
"The first-born among the gods"—the significance of this has already been explained.
This entire sacrifice is indeed so great;
the sacrifice is the self of the gods. Thus, the gods [establish] the sacrifice as their very self.

Having thus made himself the self (ātman) which is the sacrifice, he sits upon this firmament, in the heavenly world; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made himself the sacrifice, sits upon this firmament, in the heavenly world. 8.6.1.
Then he lays down the five *cūḍā* bricks.

The sacrifice is indeed the Nākasads, and the sacrifice is also the Pañcacūḍās. Now, those four officiating priests with the householder as the fifth are the Nākasads; the Hotrā-formulas are the Pañcacūḍās. That which is the Hotrā-formulas is indeed something redundant; and that which is redundant is a crest (cūḍā). Since there are five redundancies, they are therefore called the Pañcacūḍās. 8.6.1. [12]
And as to why he lays down the *nākasad* and the *pañcacūḍā* bricks:
the *nākasads* are indeed the self, and the *pañcacūḍās* are the mate.
For that which is a mate is one half of the self; when one is together with one's mate, then one is whole and complete.
For the sake of completeness (8.6.1.[13]).
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *nākasad* and *pañcacūḍā* bricks:
the *nākasads* are indeed the self (*ātman*), and the *pañcacūḍās* are offspring; [they represent] that which is redundant.
The offspring are indeed that which belongs to the self, and what is redundant is the crest (*cūḍa*).
Since there are five [bricks] in excess, they are therefore called the "Five-Crested" (*pañcacūḍā*).
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Five-Crested bricks that dwell in the firmament (*nākasat*).
The quarters are indeed the *nākasads*, and the quarters are also the *pañcacūḍās*. Those five quarters which are directed hitherward from yonder sun are the *nākasads*;
those which are directed away from it are the *pañcacūḍās*. Indeed, those quarters which are directed away from yonder sun are the redundant ones; and that which is redundant is the crest (*cūḍa*).
Because they are five in excess, therefore they are called Pañcacūḍās. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Pañcacūḍās: the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest someone..."
Thinking, "Lest the Rākṣasas and destroyers strike these worlds from above," they made these—
the *hetis* and *prahetis*— the guardians of these worlds from above.
In the same way, the sacrificer thus makes these—the missiles and counter-missiles—his guardians above these worlds. 8.6.1. [16]
He places it in front with the words, "This one in front, the golden-haired. Agni indeed is in front;
as to why he says "in front," it is because they carry forth the fire toward the east and attend upon it facing the east. And as to why he says "golden-haired," it is because he is like gold.

"Agni is the sun’s ray," for indeed the rays of Agni are like those of the sun. "Rathagṛtsa and Rathaujas are the two leaders (*senānī-grāmaṇyau*)," these are the two spring seasons. "Puñjikasthalā and Kratusthalā are the two Apsarases," so said Māhitthi; [but others say] they are the intermediate direction and the sub-direction. "The army (*senā*) and the assembly (*samiti*) are the two; biting animals are the weapon."

"Human slaughter is the weapon"—this refers to what they fear in an army or in an assembly; "fanged beasts are the weapon, human slaughter is the secondary weapon"—this refers to when they kill one another; that is human slaughter, the secondary weapon. "To them let there be homage!"—thus he pays homage to them. "May they be gracious to us!"—thus [he says]. To them [he offers salutation]. May they be gracious to us! To them [he offers salutation]. May they be gracious to us! To them [he offers salutation]. May they be gracious to us! To them [he offers salutation]. May they be gracious to us! To them [he offers salutation]. May they be gracious to us
"Thus they show mercy to him whom we hate and who hates us; we place him in their jaws.

Whomever he hates and whoever hates him, him he places in their jaws. "I place so-and-so in their jaws! he should say regarding the one he hates; then indeed there is no longer any [hope] for him. Yet, one should not pay heed to that.
For he who knows this hates only him whom he himself has designated.
8.6.1.[17] Then, on the south: "This one here is Viśvakarman, the southern. This wind here is indeed Viśvakarman.
This one indeed blows upon all this; as for why he calls it "dakṣiṇā," it is because this one blows most powerfully (*bhūyiṣṭham*) toward the south (*dakṣiṇā*).
Rathasvana and Rathecitra are its two leaders of the army and the village-clansmen; they are the two summer seasons.
Menakā and Sahajanyā are the two Apsarases; so said Māhitthi, but [according to others] these two [are the directions].

"Those sorcerers (yātudhāna) are the weapon, the Rakṣasas are the missile"—for here the sorcerers are indeed the weapon and the Rakṣasas are the missile—"to them let there be homage! The significance of this has already been explained. 8.6.1 [18].
Then, behind.

"This one behind is Viśvavyacas"—the sun, indeed, is Viśvavyacas; for when he rises, then everything here becomes spacious (*vyacas*). As to why he says "behind," therefore they see him only as he is moving westward. His chariot-bearer (*rathaprota*) and his charioteer (*asamaratha*) are the army-leader (*senānī*) and the village-chief (*grāmaṇī*).

"The two rainy seasons are the two Apsarases Pramlocantī and Anumlocantī," so said Māhitthi; "the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions. But [others say] they are day and night, for these two indeed set forth and set down again. "Tigers are the missile, snakes are the counter-missile"—for here, indeed, tigers are the missile and snakes are the counter-missile. "To them let there be homage!"—the significance of this has been explained. 8.6.1. [19]
Then from the north: "This one from the north is the possessor of wealth. Now, the sacrifice is indeed from the north;
as for why he says "from the north," it is because the sacrifice is performed from the north. And as for why he says "the possessor of wealth" (saṃyadvasu): [it is because...]
"For they lead the sacrifice; this is the wealth"—of that [sacrifice], Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi are the two leaders of the army and the hosts.

Those two are the autumnal seasons. Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī are the two Apsarases. Regarding this, Māhitthi said: "The quarters and the intermediate quarters. But for you, it is the altar and the offering-spoon.
The altar is indeed Viśvācī, and the offering-spoon is Ghṛtācī. The waters are the weapon, and the wind is the missile.

"The missile" (*praheti*)—here the waters indeed are the missile and the wind is the "after-missile" (*praheti*), for from them the wind blows hot and from them it blows cold; "to them let there be homage"—the significance of this has already been explained. 8.6.1 [20]. Now, in the middle.

"This one above, Arvāgvasu"—Parjanya, indeed, is "above," and so he says "above" because Parjanya is above; and when he says "Arvāgvasu" (possessing wealth nearby), it is because from him, wealth in the form of rain and food is bestowed nearby upon the creatures.
His two leaders of the army and the village-chiefs are Senajit and Suṣeṇa; these are the two winter seasons, and Urvaśī...
"Pūrvacitti and the two Apsarases," he said; "Dik and Upadiś," Māhitthi used to say; "Āhuti and Dakṣiṇā.
"Avasphūrjan-heti and Vidyut-praheti"—for here indeed Avasphūrjan is the *heti* and Vidyut is the *praheti*;
"to them let there be homage!"—the significance of this has been explained. 8.6.1 [21]
These indeed are your missiles and counter-missiles;
those which the gods made as guardians above these worlds, and those who were the creatures, they are your army-leaders and village-heads. And then—
That pair and those Apsarases are all these gods; having become complete and whole, together with their offspring and their mate, they settled in that vault, in the heavenly world.
In the very same way, the sacrificer, having become complete and whole, together with his offspring and his mate, settles in that vault, in the heavenly world. 8.6.1 [22]

Now, these ten bricks he lays down; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and this layer is the Virāj. But they are indeed five only, for he lays them down two by two. These are the blessings of Agni; he lays them down in the highest layer, for that highest layer is the end of Agni, and thus at the very end he utters the blessings of Agni. There are five of them, for there are five blessings in the sacrifice.
He scatters earth between them; for these two are indeed fires, lest these two bricks should burn each other.
Moreover, earth is food; thus he effects a reconciliation between the two by means of food.
Now, therefore, follows the procedure of the turning.
Having first laid them down in the east, he lays them down in the south, the west, the north, and in the middle;

then the subsequent ones, having first laid them down in the east, he lays them down in the south, the north, the middle, and in the west. For the heavenly world is indeed accessible from below; for the gods [established] these worlds from every side.
Having closed them all around from below, they entered the heavenly world; in the same way, the sacrificer here, having closed these worlds all around from below, enters the heavenly world.
He lays down the *candasyā* bricks.

Here this entire fire has been consecrated; he is here seeking glory. Indeed, prior to that, he was not capable of it—that is, he was not capable of sustaining glory. Therefore, even now people say: "He is not indeed capable of sustaining glory, nor of kingship, nor of leadership over a village. To him, the gods [bestowed] this glory.
These verses in the *candas* meters bestowed these cattle; cattle are the *candas*, and cattle are food, and food is prosperity.
8.6.2. [2] He lays down bricks in triplets.
For the animal is threefold: father, mother, and son; furthermore, the embryo, the membrane, and the afterbirth. Furthermore...
Food is threefold: cultivation, rain, and seed. There is only one *aticandā* (exceeding meter), for she alone exceeds all the meters.
She who is that prosperity (*śrī*) is that Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*), and that which is the Great Hymn consists of these very meters.
Of that [Great Hymn], the *gāyatrīs* are the head.
The *triṣṭubh* verses are the spine; the *jagatī* verses are the wings; the *paṅkti* verses are the tail.

Then, taking four syllables from each of these *kakubh* verses, he lays them down as *aticandas* verses; each of those becomes an *aticandas*. The others become *gāyatrīs*. That which is the eighty [syllables] of the *gāyatrīs* is the *bṛhatī*; that which is the *uṣṇih*s is the *bārhatī*.
The *sauṣṇiha* verses, then the *vaśa*, the two half-verses, the *aindrāgna*, and the *āvapana*—these are the *aticandas*.
Then the *nada*, the *sūdadohas*, the word-appendages (*padanuṣaṅga*), and whatever here is performed in the *anuṣṭubh* manner—all these belong to the *anuṣṭubh*.
The *dvipadā* verses are the foundation.
This indeed is the Great Hymn (mahaduktha). The Great Hymn is prosperity;
the gods bestowed this entire prosperity upon him, and in the same way, this [sacrificer] bestows this entire prosperity upon himself.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Chandasyā bricks.
The gods indeed saw this vault, the heavenly world; they entered it by means of these *stomabhāga* formulas. As they were entering, Prajāpati entered last.
That which is Prajāpati is these very *candasyā* verses. 8.6.2. [6]

The Gāyatrīs are its head. As to why they are Gāyatrīs: the head is indeed of Gāyatrī nature; there are three of them, for the head is threefold. He places them on the eastern half, for this head is in front. 8.6.2. [7]
The *triṣṭubh* verses belong to the chest.
He lays them down in the region of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; for the *pṛṣṭhas* are the two *retaḥsic*s, and the *pṛṣṭhas* rest upon the chest.
The *jagatī* verses are the hips.

As far as he places the *triṣṭubh* verses behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, so far behind does he place the *jagatīs*. For this *svayamātṛṇṇā* is that vital breath which is here in the middle; as far as it extends...
From this vital breath, the *purastāduras* [bricks] are in front; the *paścācroṇī* [bricks] are behind.
The *anuṣṭubh* verses are the two thighs. He places them immediately adjacent to the *jagatī* verses; he places them immediately adjacent to the *paścācroṇī* [bricks].
He places the *sakthya* verses; the *bṛhatī*s are the ribs, and the *kakubh*s are the vertebrae; thus, between the *triṣṭubh*s and the *kakubh*s—
He lays down *bṛhatī* bricks; therefore these ribs are fastened on both sides, to the *kīkasās* and to the *jatrus*.
The *uṣṇih*s are the necks;
he lays them down immediately after the *gāyatrī*s, for the necks are not separated from the head.
He places [them]. 8.6.2.[12] The wings are *pañkti* verses. As to why they are *pañkti* verses: the wings are fivefold (*pāṅktau*), and he lays them down on both sides.
These two wings are on the sides; he places that *canda* which is larger on the south, for he thereby makes the right half of the animal more powerful;
therefore the right half of the animal is more powerful.
The *aticanda* is the belly.
The meters (*candāṃsi*) are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; the belly eats food, for it is the belly that eats food.
Therefore, when food reaches the belly, it then becomes consumed and its form is exhausted.
Since this [deity] eats the cattle, which are the meters, she is called *Atticandā*; indeed, she is *Atticandā* because she eats the meters. Thus she is *Aticandā*.
Thus they speak cryptically, for the gods desire what is cryptic.
The womb is the earthy layer;
he places these two in contact, for the belly and the womb are in contact.
The two [bricks] joined by *purīṣa* are for you; indeed, feces (*purīṣa*) is flesh (*māṃsa*), and by means of flesh both the belly and the womb are joined together.
The first is an *aticandā*, the other is *purīṣavat*; for the belly is above and the womb is below.
He lays them down facing the east.
For this fire-altar is built facing the east; moreover, the belly is indeed in front, and the womb faces the east.
Outside the *stomabhāgas* is the heart; for the *stomabhāgas* are the heart, and the heart is indeed above the belly, and the womb is below.
He places them to the south of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
Then, in the first layer, he places the *udara* and the *yoni* to the north of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; for that which is this vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the middle is indeed this [brick].
The *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick provides for this vital breath (*prāṇa*); on both sides of it, she establishes the belly and the womb.
Therefore, on both sides of this vital breath are the belly and the womb.
The two-footed verses are the support.

In that they consist of two-footed verses, it is because a pair is a foundation; there are three, for a triad is a foundation. He places them behind, for what is behind is a foundation. This, then, is his well-made self.

Now, for whomsoever they thus fashion this self as well-made, he indeed comes into being with that self as well-made; but for whomsoever they fashion it otherwise than this, they make his self ill-made, and he indeed comes into being with that self as ill-made. 8.6.2. [19]
Therefore, these two *sāman*-concluding phrases (*nidhana*) are recited:

"The *arka* of the gods in the highest heaven; the gods of the *arka* in the highest heaven. For when the gods were entering [the body], Prajāpati entered as the last; therefore it is said, "The *arka* of the gods."

Regarding the phrase "in the highest heaven": when he says, "of the *arka* (the sun), O gods, in the highest heaven," this fire is indeed the *arka*. All the gods are contained within its highest layer (*citi*); therefore he says, "of the *arka*, O gods, in the highest heaven.
He lays down the Gārhapatya fire-altar.

Indeed, having obtained this, the gods thought, "We have succeeded. They said, "By what means have we succeeded in this? They replied, "By the Gārhapatya alone. Having built the Gārhapatya and ascended it, they [attained their goal].

"We have seen the first layer; from the first, the second; from the second, the third; from the third, the fourth; from the fourth, the fifth; from the fifth, this [world]," they said. They then spoke: "Consider how this success may be established among us alone. They—
When they said, "Be mindful," they were indeed saying, "Seek a layer (citi)," meaning, "Seek that whereby this success might be established among us. As they were thus reflecting, they [proceeded].
Seeing this, they said, "Let us bring this one here and place it down. They brought it here and placed it down.

Regarding it, they disputed: the Vasus from the east, the Rudras from the south, the Ādityas from the west, the Maruts from the north, and the Viśve Devas from above, each saying, "Let us place it here! Let us place it here! 8.6.3 [4]
They said, "Let us place it right in the middle; being placed in the middle, it shall belong to all of us. They placed it in the middle. Thus they placed that success within themselves;
from the very center, from the very middle, they placed that success within themselves. In the same way, the sacrificer [does so].
In that he lays down the Gārhapatya fire-altar, he thereby places this very attainment within himself; by laying it down in the middle, he places this attainment within himself right in the middle.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Gārhapatya fire-altar...
The Gārhapatya is indeed food, and this built-up Agni is the eater;
he thus places that food upon it. By placing it in the middle, he places that food in his very middle. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Gārhapatya...
The sacrificial altar (vedī) is indeed the world of the gods; now, this [fire-altar] is built outside the altar.
When he brings it here and lays it down, he thereby establishes it upon the altar in the world of the gods.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Gārhapatya fire.
The lotus leaf is indeed the womb; now, this [fire-altar] is built outside the womb.
Indeed, that work of the fire-altar which is performed prior to the lotus leaf is outside the womb.
When he brings it here and lays it down, he thereby establishes it in its womb, upon the lotus leaf; and thus indeed does this [fire] become established.

On the outside he lays down eight bricks; their significance has been explained. He builds that very [altar] with these same sacrificial formulas and in this same manner. For that which was yonder is indeed this one; having brought that very thing here, he lays it down. 8.6.3.
Then he lays down the *punaściti* (re-building layer).
The gods, having piled this Gārhapatya fire-altar, did not perceive success in it; for the piling of the Gārhapatya is a womb, and the success of a womb is the seed and progeny.
In that womb, they did not perceive the seed or progeny. 8.6.3 [9]
They said, "Consider how we may place seed and procreation in this womb.
They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek how we may place seed and procreation in this womb. 8.6.3. [10]

As they were reflecting, they perceived this further layer of consciousness; they laid it down. Thus, in this womb, they placed the seed of procreation; from the very center, from the very center, they placed that seed in this womb.

In the same way, when the sacrificer piles the *punar-citi* (re-piling), he places procreative seed in this very womb; he places procreative seed in the middle of this womb, right in its center. 8.6.3. [11]

Some indeed place it on the hind part [of the altar], saying, "From the hind part, semen is emitted; at the junction of the tail, from the tail, semen is emitted. One should not do so; for they thus place the semen and procreation outside the womb.
Those who do so in that manner would place it in the very middle; thus he now places the seed and procreation in the womb.
He lays down eight bricks.
The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as his [extent]...
By that much he pours him out as seed; he settles it five times.

The fire-altar consists of five layers, the year has five seasons, and Agni is the year: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he pours him out as seed. There are eight bricks; he settles them five times, which makes thirteen.

Thirteen months are a year; there are thirteen layers of earth for the fire-altar. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does this become. Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *punaściti* (re-piling).

Indeed, he does what is improper when he piles the Gārhapatya fire-altar higher than the Āhavanīya; therefore, when he lays down the *punar-citi* (re-piling), he brings back that very Agni which was already piled and piles it again upon it. Thus, since it is already piled...
Because he piles it again, it is called the "re-piling" (punaściti).
Regarding this, some place the Gārhapatya fire on the rear half [of the altar] and the re-piling on the front half, saying, "These two are indeed the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya;
these two fires are thus [separated]. One should not do so; for the Gārhapatya is indeed this world.
The Āhavanīya fire is the sky; for that [sky] is above this [earth]. Therefore, he should lay it down only higher [than the Gārhapatya].
And furthermore, when he lays down both the Gārhapatya and the *punaściti*, these two are indeed the altar (*vedi*) and the high-altar (*uttaravedi*) of Agni. Thus...
Those which he previously scattered for the sacrifice—these indeed are those of Agni; thus, when he has laid down these two, he places Agni upon them.
He thereby establishes him both on the *veda* and on the high altar (*uttaravedi*).
And as to why he further lays down the *punaściti* (re-piling).

This is indeed a repeated sacrifice; this is a subsequent worship of the gods. Verily, he thus lays down a repeated sacrifice and a subsequent worship of the gods; towards him the repeated sacrifice inclines.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *punar-citi* (re-piling):

that very Agni whom the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the seers (*ṛṣi*), first constructed—that same one he now piles up again. Because he piles him again when he has already been piled, it is therefore called the *punar-citi*. 8.6.3. [18]

"With that austerity by which the seers entered the sacrificial session"—this refers to those very seers. "Kindling the fire, they brought the light"—this means that while kindling the fire, they brought the heavenly world. "In that firmament I have placed the fire."

"Heaven indeed is the world, the firmament which they call 'the one for whom the sacrificial grass is strewn by the Manavas'—those who are wise are the Manavas for whom the sacrificial grass is strewn.
He is indeed always one for whom the sacrificial grass is strewn.
O gods, may we follow him with our wives.

"May we follow him with all this—with sons, or brothers, or even with gold"—this is what he means. "Seizing the firmament (nāka) in the world of the well-done"—the firmament is indeed the heavenly world;
thus, "seizing the heavenly world in the world of the well-done," [he says] upon the third ridge in the luminous realm of heaven.
"This indeed is the third back of the luminous sky, where he now burns"—this is the middle of speech, for this is where he is piled up.
"The active one has ascended to the middle of speech.
This indeed is the middle of speech, where he is now being built.
"Bhuraṇyu" means "the sustainer. "This Agni is the lord of the good, the wise one" means "this Agni is the protector of the virtuous, the one who makes them conscious.

"Established on the back of the earth, shining brightly" means "established on the back of the earth, blazing. "May they place those who fight us under our feet" means "may they cast those who seek to harm us beneath our feet."
"All evils"— this refers to that.
"This Agni is the most heroic, the bestower of vigor"—
this means "this Agni is the most powerful, the bestower of vigor," he who is thousandfold.
"Shining forth, never failing"—this means "shining forth, being vigilant. "Radiant in the midst of the flood"—the flood is indeed these worlds;
thus, this means "blazing in these worlds. "Approach the celestial abodes"—this means "go forward to the heavenly world. 8.6.3 [22]

"Fall down together, go forth together toward him"—this he says to those seers: "Fall down together toward him and go forth together toward him. "O Agni, prepare the paths leading to the gods"—just as [before].

"The *yajus* likewise provides the connection: 'Creating the parents again as young,' for speech and mind are the parents, and these two, speech and mind, have entered these two fires. 'In you this thread [is stretched],' he says this of that thread which was woven by the seers. (8.6.3)
"Wake up, O Agni; do thou watch over us"—with these words he addresses this very Agni, saying, "Wake up loudly for him and watch over him.
"May you two unite with this man through his sacrifices and pious works"—just as the sacrificial formula is, so it is.
"A kinsman in this assembly, and in the one above"—the sky, indeed, is the assembly above;
"may the All-Gods and the sacrificer sit down," he thereby causes the sacrificer to sit together with the All-Gods. (8.6.3) "With that by which you carry a thousand..."
"O Agni, by that [path] through which one wins all possessions"—this is indeed his most firmly established abode.
"By which he carries a thousand, by which he carries all possessions; by that, lead this sacrifice of ours to heaven among the gods.
By that, lead this sacrifice of ours to the heavenly world among the gods—this is what he says. "This is yours..."
"The womb at the proper season"—its significance has been explained. He lays down eight bricks; their significance has also been explained. 8.7.1.
[1] He lays down the seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks. These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons he lays down. This, then, is the whole.
As to why they are the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*): the seasonal bricks are the year, and the year is all this;
thus he lays down all this. Moreover, it is procreation; for the seasonal bricks are the year, and the year is procreation; thus he lays down procreation. 8.7.1. [2]
Moreover, as to why he lays down the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*):
