They entered [the sacrifice] by means of their forms, one season after another; therefore, in each single season, the form of all the seasons is present.
That they have various beginnings is because they were created separately; but that they have a common conclusion is because they entered by means of their forms. 8.7.1.
He lays them down.

*Tapaḥ* and *Tapasya* are the names of the two winter seasons (*śaiśira-ṛtū*). It is by these very names that he lays them down. Yonder sun, indeed, is *tapaḥ*; therefore these two seasons are not separated from it. Because these two seasons are not separated from him, they are called *tapaḥ* and *tapasyaḥ*. 8.7.1. [6]
"Thou art the inner bond of Agni.
This Agni is the year; he is joined together by the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). Thus, he extends and unites the year with the seasons. "May Heaven and Earth be in order; may the waters be in order."
"O plants!"—by this he thus prepares all this by means of the seasons. "May the fires, being of one mind, be fit for pre-eminence; homage to them!"—for these bricks are indeed separate fires;
he says this so that they may be fit for the pre-eminence of these two seasons, those fires which are between them and are of one mind.

"These two, heaven and earth"—as the *yajus* formula is, so is its significance. "May these two winter seasons, being well-disposed, settle around [this fire] as the gods settled around Indra"—just as the gods settled around Indra, so may these two seasons settle around it for the sake of preeminence. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months.
He settles it once; he thereby makes that one season.
Now, as to why he lays these two down here:
this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds; of him, the sky alone—

The fifth layer is the sky; the cool season is its season. In that he lays these two bricks here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this part of his body; therefore he lays these two here.
Furthermore, as to why he lays these two here...

This Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year; his head indeed is the fifth layer, for the cold season (śiśira) is his head. In that he places these two bricks here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this body of his; therefore he places these two here. 8.7.1. [9]
He places the two seasonal bricks in front of both the *svayamātṛṇā* and the *viśvajyotis*.
The *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed the highest [brick], being the sky; the *viśvajyotis* is the highest, being the sun. Thus, he establishes the seasons between the sky and the sun.

Therefore, the seasons and the generative power are indeed closer to this [earth]. He thus bestows the generative power of both the sky and the sun closer to this [earth]; therefore, offspring are born closer to this [earth]. Indeed, the generative power beyond this is fixed; for as many gods as there were in the beginning, so many gods there are now. 8.7.1. [10]
Then, he places the two seasonal bricks above the first naturally-perforated brick and the first Viśvajyotis brick;
for this earth is indeed the first naturally-perforated brick, and Agni is the first Viśvajyotis.
The Viśvajyotis [bricks] place the seasons above that; therefore, from here upwards are the seasons.
Moreover, this is procreation; he places procreation upwards from here, and therefore offspring are procreated only upwards from here.
One should not displace them.
"One should not displace the seasonal bricks," they say; for indeed, when one dies, the seasons are displaced for him.
Therefore, wherever he lays down the first two, there he should lay down all of them. Moreover, these worlds are indeed the seasonal bricks.

With these he piles up those worlds above; moreover, the seasonal bricks are the ruling power (*kṣatra*), so he piles up the ruling power above with the layers; moreover, the seasonal bricks are the year, so he piles up the year above with the layers. He does not pile them with any other [brick].
One should place [the bricks] upon the *yajuṣmatī* bricks, thinking, "Lest I place the Kṣatra over the Viś.
These, indeed, are the *saṃyānī* bricks.
For this, the gods...

By means of the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*), they [the ancient sacrificers] united these worlds—those above from here and those below from there; in the very same way, the sacrificer now unites these worlds by means of the seasonal bricks—those above from here and those below from there. 8.7.1.
Now, indeed, the Caraka-Adhvaryus say:
They place them down saying, "These are indeed different *saṃyānī* bricks"; one should not do so, for they would thereby cause an excess; these very ones are the *saṃyānī*s. 8.7.1.
[15] Then he places the *viśvajyotis* brick.
The Āditya is indeed the last Viśvajyotis, for the Āditya alone is the all-light in yonder world;
it is the Āditya that he thus lays down. And as to why he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick:
Offspring, indeed, is the Viśvajyotis; for offspring is indeed the universal light.
He thus lays down this [brick] as procreation.
8.7.1. He lays down the Viśvajyotis brick to the east of the Svayamātṛṇṇā.

The sky is indeed the highest *svayamātṛṇṇā*, and the sun is the highest *viśvajyotis*; he thus places the sun below the sky, and therefore this [sun] shines directed hitherward. Moreover, this is procreation; he thus establishes the procreative power of the sky directed hitherward.
Therefore, from this, only that which is proximate is produced.
8.7.1 [18]. Now, upon the first naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇā*), he places the Viśvajyotis brick above it; for this earth is indeed...

The first [brick] is the *svayamātṛṇā*, the fire; the first is the *viśvajyotis*. From here he places the fire upwards; therefore the fire blazes upwards from here. Moreover, this is procreation: from here he places procreation upwards; therefore offspring are born upwards from here. 8.7.1. [19]
Then, upon the middle *svayamātṛṇā* brick, he places the *viśvajyotis* brick on top.
The middle *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and the middle *viśvajyotis* is Vāyu; thus he places Vāyu in the intermediate space.
Therefore, this wind is in the intermediate space.
These are those very lights.
In that he lays them down in this manner, he thereby places these very lights together in proper alignment.
Therefore, from here upwards the fire blazes; downwards yonder sun shines in the atmosphere; and this wind blows crosswise.
"May Parameṣṭhin settle thee"—for Parameṣṭhin indeed [settled] this fifth [layer].
He saw the altar on the back of the sky as "the luminous one," for on the back of the sky is that luminous Āditya.
[He offers] "for all out-breathing, for in-breathing, for diffused breathing";
for the Viśvajyotis is indeed the breath, and it is for all this.
"May the breath go to the universal light; may it go to all the light"—this is what he says. "The sun is your overlord"—he thus makes the sun her overlord.
Having set it down, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has already been explained. 8.7.1 [23]
These indeed are the *saṃyānī* bricks.
For by means of these *viśvajyotis* bricks, the gods reached these worlds—from here upwards and from there downwards; in the same way, the sacrificer [does so].

"By means of the *viśvajyotis* [bricks], he thus traverses these worlds—those above and those below, as well as those behind and those in front. 8.7.1. [24] Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus lay down other bricks called *saṃyānīs*, but one should not do so; it would indeed be excessive.
These very [bricks] are the *saṃyānī*s; 8.7.2.
Then he lays down the *lokampṛṇā* brick.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the *lokampṛṇā*. This...
He fills these worlds; he thus lays down that very sun. He lays it down in all the layers; for these layers are indeed these worlds.
He thus places that sun in these worlds; therefore, he shines upon all these worlds. 8.7.2. [2]
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Lokampṛṇā brick:

the Lokampṛṇā is the nobility (kṣatra), and these other bricks are the common people (viś). He thus places the nobility among the common people. He lays it down in all the layers; he thereby places it among the entire common people.
It bestows one who intoxicates the *kṣatra*.
This [verse] is indeed one; it makes that *kṣatra* concentrated in one place and prosperity concentrated in one place. Now, as for the second [verse]:
That pair is indeed half of this self; for when one is together with a mate, then one is whole and complete.

For the sake of completeness, he lays down many bricks with a single *yajus* formula; thereby he bestows power upon the ruling class (*kṣatra*) by means of its own strength, making the ruling class more powerful than the common people (*viś*). Then the others [the bricks] are separate and distinct.
He lays them down with *yajus* formulas; he thereby makes the people weaker than the ruling power, speaking discordantly and having divided minds.
He lays down the first two in this corner;
he thereby places that sun in this direction.
He moves from here to there, and from there back to here; he moves from here to there, and from there back to here; he moves from here to there, and from there back to here;
he moves from here to there, and from there back to here.
Now, if he places them right there at the first layer—
He should place it on the uppermost layer all at once; for that sun, having traversed these worlds, does not overstep them. Having removed the former ones, he places it on the uppermost layer;
he thereby causes that sun to overstep these worlds. Therefore, that sun is not stationary throughout these worlds.
Moving to the right, he goes around again and again:
"Fill the space, fill the gap!"— that is to say,
"Fill the space and fill the gap," and then, "Sit down as a firm foundation."

"Thou art," he says; "sit thou firm," that is, "be thou firmly established. "Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati have seated thee in this womb"—that is, "Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati have caused thee to stand firm in this womb.
He does so with an Anuṣṭubh verse; for the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and Indra is speech; and the Lokampṛṇā is Indra.
He settles it, for this [brick] is not yet settled; he recites with the *sūdadohas* verse. The *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
by means of the vital breath he thus makes it continuous and joins it together.
8.7.2. Regarding this they say: "How does this *lokampṛṇā* become one whose course is unexhausted? It is yonder sun.
This Lokampṛṇā is indeed the far-reaching; moreover, speech is the Lokampṛṇā, for speech is indeed far-reaching.
Having laid down the Yajuṣmatī bricks, he covers them with the Lokampṛṇā; for the Yajuṣmatī bricks are food.
The self is the *lokampṛṇā* brick; he encloses that food with the self. Therefore, food, being enclosed by the self, becomes the self itself.
8.7.2 [9] That indeed is within the self alone.
He lays down the *yajuṣmatī* bricks, but not on the wings or the tail; he thus places that food in the self (*ātman*).

For when food is placed in the self, it protects the self as well as the wings and the tail; but when it is placed on the wings and the tail, it protects neither the self nor the wings and the tail. 8.7.2 [10]
He places both the *yajuṣmatī* bricks and the *lokampṛṇā* bricks upon the body;
therefore, this body is double-layered and, as it were, more substantial.
He places only the *lokampṛṇā* bricks in the wings and tail; therefore, the wings and tail are, as it were, thinner. And he places them lengthwise.
He lays them down crosswise within the body; for bricks are indeed bones, and therefore these bones in the body are both longitudinal and transverse.
In the wings and tail, however, they are laid down only lengthwise, for there is no transverse bone at all in the wings and tail.
This, then, is the distinction between what is built up (*cita*) and what is not built up (*acita*): thus is that which is built up, and otherwise is that which is not built up.
He indeed covers the *svayamātṛṇā* brick with the *lokampṛṇā*.
The *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the *lokampṛṇā* is the sun;
he thus kindles the vital breath by means of the sun. Therefore, this vital breath is warm, and by that [brick] he [covers] his entire self.
It covers everything; it kindles itself with the sun. Therefore, this entire self is warm.
This, indeed, is the sign of one who will live and one who will die: one who will live is warm, while one who will die is cold. 8.7.2. [12]
In whichever corner he first lays down [the bricks],
from there he proceeds, covering them by tens, as far as the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; then, turning to the right, he proceeds behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, covering them as far as the *anūkyā*.
Then, returning again, he covers that boundary.
He first covers himself;
for of one being born, it is indeed the self that is born first, and then the right [side].

Then the wing, then the tail; it moves to the right, for that is the way among the gods. Moreover, in this very manner, yonder sun moves around these worlds from left to right. This *lokapṛṇā* brick is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
With it, he covers his entire self;

in his entire self, he places the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For if this [brick] were not to reach a certain limb of his, the vital breath would not reach that limb of his; and whatever limb the vital breath does not reach, that indeed withers away.
It withers away; therefore, one should cover it entirely with this [bricks].
He piles the wings and the tail from out of the body itself;
for from the body itself the limbs grow forth. Then...
If one were to place them facing downward from the front, it would be as if one were replacing a limb after having brought it from elsewhere; such would that be.
One should not place a broken one nor a black one.
For that which is broken indeed suffers; this form is one that has suffered.
Thinking, "Lest I should construct myself as afflicted," he does not throw out a brick that is unbroken;

thinking, "Lest I should place what is unafflicted outside of myself," having counted them back from the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), those bricks which exceed the *virāj* should not be placed further north. Indeed, they are praised; having broken them, he throws them onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
Or rather, he should throw it out as rubbish; for rubbish is the resting place of what is redundant.
Thus, he establishes these very [bricks] in that which is the resting place of the redundant.
Now, therefore, regarding the measurements of the bricks themselves.

One should place bricks measuring a foot in length on the first and the last layers; for the foot is indeed a foundation, and that which is the foot is also the hand. The tallest bricks should be those measuring the height of the thighs, for there is no bone taller than the thighs. There should be three layers marked with three lines, for they are threefold.
"Verily, these worlds are two, the Unmeasured and the Written; these two layers are indeed essence, for essence is indeed unmeasured.
However, all [layers] should have three lines written upon them, for all these worlds are indeed threefold. 8.7.2.
Now, therefore, regarding the insertion of the bricks themselves.

Whatever brick one knows to be *yajuṣmatī*, that one should place in the middle layer; for the middle layer is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and the intermediate space is the receptacle of all beings. Moreover, the *yajuṣmatī* bricks are food, and the middle layer is the belly.

He places that food within the belly of the *cit*. Regarding this, they say: "One should not place them, lest one should make an excess. Yet, one should indeed place them; for these bricks are placed for the sake of desires, and there is no such thing as an excess of desires. However, he should not place them at all; for this much indeed is what the gods [performed].
Not doing so [as previously described], he then scatters loose earth (purīṣa).
For loose earth is indeed flesh; with flesh he thus covers this brick.
Having placed the bricks upon it, he covers that bone with flesh. He indeed scatters [the earth] upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick;
for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is breath, and the loose soil (*purīṣa*) is food; thus he places that food within the breath.
He places it; thereby he covers his entire self. Therefore, whatever food is placed within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it protects his entire self and pervades his entire self.
Some, however, say that one should not scatter [the seeds] upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
"The *svayamātṛṇā* brick is the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
[he thinks], 'Lest I should shut off the vital breaths. He should indeed sow it; for the vital breaths are supported by food. Indeed, the vital breaths of one who does not eat food fail."

They grow for him in that way, just as dry metal images become hollow; indeed, he comes into being in yonder world like that. Therefore, one should sow only upon the *svayamātṛṇā* brick. Having sown upon the *svayamātṛṇā* brick—
Covering [the altar] along the spine, he goes as far as the enclosing stones;
turning to the right, he goes covering the space behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone back to the spine. First, he covers the body [of the altar].
For the self indeed arises first for one being born, then the right wing, then the tail, then the left wing; that is a movement to the right, for such is the way among the gods.
This very purīṣa is breath itself.
By that, he covers his entire self;

in its entirety, he places the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within that self. For if he were not to reach this limb of his with it, the vital breath would not reach that limb of his; and whatever limb the vital breath does not reach, that indeed withers away.
It withers away; therefore, one should cover it entirely with this [verse]:
"All beings have magnified Indra," for all beings indeed cause Indra to grow, he who is as vast as the ocean.
"Gira"—by this he speaks of his greatness; "the best charioteer among charioteers," for he is indeed the best charioteer among charioteers;
"the lord of strengths, the lord of the true"—strengths (*vāja*) are indeed food, so it means "the lord of foods, the lord of the true.
He scatters [the earth] with an *anuṣṭubh* verse addressed to Indra, for the loose soil (*purīṣa*) belongs to Indra.
Now, this is half of Agni: that which is the loose soil (*purīṣa*) is one half, and that which consists of bricks (*iṣṭaka*) is the other half.

Regarding this they say: "Since he lays down the bricks with all the meters and with all the deities, yet he pours down this [loose soil] with a single verse addressed to a single deity, how is this the other half of Agni?"—[The answer is: "Indra, indeed..."
In that he scatters [the earth] with a verse addressed to Indra, he thereby establishes this half of Agni;
and in that he does so with an *anuṣṭubh*—for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech comprises all the meters—he thereby establishes the other half.
Then he lays down the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā brick.

The Vikarṇī is indeed Vāyu; the Svayamātṛṇā is the highest heaven. He thus lays down both Vāyu and the heaven. He lays them down on the topmost layer, for Vāyu and the heaven are at the topmost [layer].
He lays them down touching each other, for Vāyu and the heaven are in contact with each other. [He places] the former...
He lays down the *vikarṇī* brick; he thereby places Vāyu from the sky towards this world, and therefore this wind blows hitherward.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *vikarṇī* brick...

Or rather, where they cause the horse to smell the layer, there that sun strings these worlds together on a thread; and that which is the thread is Vāyu. Now, that which is Vāyu is this same Vikarṇī brick.
Therefore, when he lays this down, it is that very sun who strings these worlds together on a thread. 8.7.3. [11]
Moreover, as to why he lays down both the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā:

the Vikarṇī is indeed life-span (āyus) and the Svayamātṛṇā is breath (prāṇa); thus he lays down both life-span and breath. He lays them down in the highest [layer], for life-span and breath are in the highest [place].

For as each [brick] is touched, life-span (*āyus*) and breath (*prāṇa*) [are established]; he places the eastern and the northern *vikarṇī* bricks; by means of life-span, he thus encompasses breath on both sides.
"Like a neighing horse in a meadow... (RV 10.146.2).
"When he has emerged from the great enclosure, then the wind blows after his flame;
and then, indeed, thy path becomes black. When the wind blows after his flame, then his path becomes black.
He lays it down with a *triṣṭubh* verse, for Vāyu is connected with the *triṣṭubh*; [he uses] an *āgneyī* verse, for this is a rite pertaining to Agni.
[He places it] with the unexpressed [formula], for the wind is indeed unexpressed; and when he says "the wind," he means the wind.
8.7.3.[13] Then he lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with [the formula]:
"In the seat of Ayu I settle thee. This indeed...
"Life, its seat is this; it protects," for he indeed protects all this. "And in the path of life," for all this is in the path of his life.
"Of the ocean, this is the heart; the radiant, the shining," for the sky is radiant and shining.
"By which you shine upon the sky, the earth, and the broad atmosphere," for such indeed is he.
"It illumines these worlds.
"May Parameṣṭhin settle you"—
for Parameṣṭhin indeed beheld this fifth layer.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down [the brick] with Parameṣṭhin:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, the deities took him and departed; Parameṣṭhin, having taken his head, stepped aside and stood apart. 8.7.3 [16]
He said to him:
"Come to me and give me that by which you have departed from me. [The other asked: "What will be mine from that? [He replied:
"That part of my self (ātman) shall belong to you as having you as its deity. "So be it," he said.

In this regard, Parameṣṭhin established this [brick] therein. Now, that which is the last *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated brick) is that very part of his own self; therefore, he places it here at this point.
Whatever belongs to this self, that he now restores to it; therefore, he places this brick here.
"On the back of heaven, wide-extending, broad-extending," for this is indeed the back of heaven.
"Extensive and wide as the sky, support the sky; do not harm the sky"—this means "support yourself, support yourself;
do not harm yourself. For the sake of every out-breath and in-breath. 8.7.3. [19]

"For the diffused breath, for the upward breath"—the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇā*) is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the vital breath serves as a support for all this; "for stability, for movement"—these worlds are indeed the naturally perforated bricks, and these worlds are stability and movement; "may Sūrya protect thee"—that is, "may Sūrya guard thee"; "with great well-being."

"Greatly with well-being"—this [means] "with the most peaceful heart-protecting cover"; by "the most peaceful heart-protecting cover," he means "by that which is the most peaceful heart-protecting cover.
He lays them down separately;
for wind and heaven are separate. He settles them once; he thereby makes them common, he makes them the same.

Life-breath (*āyus*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*): these two indeed become the two pebbles; both are self-perforated, for life-breath and vital breath are the same. Then he consecrates them with the *sūdadohas* verse. The *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath; by means of the vital breath he thus connects and joins them together. 8.7.3. [21]
"Those [waters] of his, yielding the pressed juice (*sūdadohas*).

Water, indeed, is the *sūda*; food is the "milking. "They mix the Soma, the speckled ones (*pṛśnayaḥ*). Food, indeed, is the speckled one. "At the birth of the gods (*janman devānām*). The year, indeed, is the birth of the gods. "The clans (*viśaḥ*). The sacrifice, indeed, is the clans; for in the sacrifice—
"All beings are entered into the three luminous realms of heaven"—the three pressings are indeed the three luminous realms; by this he refers to the pressings.

With an *anuṣṭubh* verse [he does this], for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). By means of speech and vital breath, he thus makes them continuous and joins them together. This very *sūdadohas* verse, though being one, accompanies all the bricks; it is the vital breath.
Verily, they are the *sūdadohas* verses; therefore, this single vital breath (*prāṇa*), though being one, moves through all the limbs and the entire body.
8.7.4. Then he sings the *Sāmans* upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks.
These worlds, indeed, are the *svayamātṛṇā* bricks; they are these pebbles. Having laid them down, the gods saw them as being just like this—just as these dry pebbles are.
They said, "Find out how we may establish enjoyment and sustenance in these worlds. Thus they spoke.

When they said, "Reflect! (cetayadhvam), they were indeed saying, "Seek a layer" (citim icata); that is, "Seek it so that we may place within these worlds the essence and the means of subsistence. 8.7.4 [3] While they were thus reflecting, they said:
Seeing these *sāmans* as common [to all], they sang them; by means of them, they placed within these worlds the essence that serves as sustenance.
In the same way, when the sacrificer sings these *sāmans*, he places within these very worlds the essence that serves as sustenance. 8.7.4. [4]
He sings over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks.
These worlds, indeed, are the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s; it is thus that he places within these very worlds essence and sustenance. 8.7.4[5]

He sings over these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*), namely *bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *svar*. *Bhūr* is indeed this world, *bhuvas* is the intermediate space, and *svar* is yonder world. Thus, he places essence and sustenance within these very worlds. 8.7.4 [6]

These indeed have different preludes (prastāva) but the same finale (nidhana). As to why they have different preludes, it is because they saw them as distinct; and as to why they have the same finale, it is because there is indeed only one foundation for the sacrifice and only one finale.
"Heaven itself is the world; therefore, they have *svar* as their light and *nidhana*. 8.7.4.[7] Then he sprinkles it with pieces of gold.
At this point, this entire fire has been consecrated; in it, the gods..."
They placed this supreme immortal form within him; in the same way, he now places this supreme immortal form within him.
Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles him with chips of gold:
Verily, he thus places that delightful body in the middle of this [altar], both the gold plate and the man;
then he covers this whole thing from above with a delightful body. 8.7.4. [9]
By two hundred each;
the sacrificer has two feet, and Agni is the sacrificer:
as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he bestows this supreme immortal form upon him.
Five times [he offers], for the fire-altar consists of five layers; there are five seasons, and the year is the fire-altar.
As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—with just that much he bestows upon it this immortal, supreme form.
With a thousand [offerings], for a thousand is everything; with everything indeed he bestows upon it this immortal, supreme form. 8.7.4. [10]
Standing behind [the fire], facing east;

then from the north, facing south; then from the front, facing west; then, having gone around by the rear, standing on the south side, facing north—that is the clockwise direction (dakṣiṇāvṛt), for that is the way among the gods; then, having gone around again, [he stands] behind, facing east.
While standing, he says: "Truly, this [work] has already been performed by him in the past.

(8.7.4[11]) "Thou art the measure of a thousand; thou art the counterpart of a thousand; thou art the standard of a thousand; thou art a thousandfold; for a thousand, thee! (sahasrasya pramāsi / sahasrasya pratimāsi sahasrasyonmāsi sāhasro 'si sahasrāya tveti).
"Verily, the thousand is everything; you are everything; for everything, you!"—this is what it means.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the layers (*citi*) and the fillings (*purīṣa*):
this very world is the first layer, and cattle are the filling.

In that he covers the first layer with loose soil (*purīṣa*), he covers this world with cattle. The second layer is indeed the intermediate space; birds are the loose soil. In that he covers the second layer with loose soil...
He covers the atmosphere with its birds; thus he covers it.
The third layer is indeed the sky;
the stars are the loose earth (*purīṣa*). When he covers the third layer with loose earth, [he covers the sky with the stars].
He covers that with the stars;

the fourth layer is the sacrifice itself, and the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are the loose soil. When he covers the fourth layer with loose soil, [he covers] the sacrifice with the sacrificial gifts.
He covers that sacrifice with the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
The sacrificer himself is the fifth layer;
offspring is the loose soil (purīṣa); in that he covers the fifth layer with loose soil, [he provides for offspring].
He covers the sacrificer with offspring by means of that.
The sixth layer is indeed the heavenly world;
the gods are the *purīṣa* (filling soil) when they cover the sixth layer with *purīṣa*.
It covers the heaven; it covers that world with the gods.
The seventh layer is indeed immortality; he places that as the highest. He thus bestows immortality upon this whole [universe] as its highest;
therefore, immortality is the highest of this whole [universe]. Therefore the gods are not separated from it, and therefore they are immortal.
Thus with reference to the deities. Now with reference to the self: that which is this foundation and this downward breath—that is the first layer, the flesh.

When he covers the first layer with loose soil (*purīṣa*), he thereby covers that part of the self with flesh. Having laid down the bricks, the bricks are the bones; he thus covers those bones with flesh.
He does not cover them from below; therefore these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are not covered from below, but rather from above.

He covers this; he covers the upper part of this self with flesh; therefore, this upper part of his self is covered with flesh and leaves no space. (8.7.4 [20]) That which is above the foundation and below the middle.
The second layer is his flesh;
when he covers the second layer with loose soil, he thereby covers that part of his self with flesh.
Having laid down the bricks—which are the bones—he then covers those bones with flesh by means of the loose soil.
He places [the bricks] and covers them with loose soil; thus he covers this body of his on both sides with flesh.
Therefore, this body of his is covered on both sides with flesh and leaves no space.
The third layer is indeed the middle.

That which is above the middle and below the neck is the fourth layer; the neck itself is the fifth layer; the head itself is the sixth layer; and the vital breaths themselves are the seventh layer. He places that [seventh layer] last; he thereby places the vital breaths as the highest part of this entire [body]. Therefore, of this [body],...

The vital breaths are supreme for everyone; he places the loose soil (purīṣa) [on top], for the loose soil is indeed flesh; by means of flesh he thus establishes the vital breaths. He does not cover them over from above; therefore these vital breaths are not covered over from above.
